speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: MR. WHELAN-ALLEGED INADEQUATE REPORTING BY PRESS OF SPEECH MADE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. In the debate on Friday, March 14, I was the final speaker. I spoke concerning criticism, and so on, which was levelled at the Minister of Agriculture. I rise on this question of privilege not because of lack of reporting but lack of printing what I actually said. It makes me wonder how far we can go. This question of privilege affects many members of the House of Commons because of the impression that is left. For example, in the March 15 edition of the Ottawa Journal, all that I could find reported about me was a brief article headlined, "Whelan defends speaking tours". I quote from the article:
"Too many damn politicians hole up in this place and forget there's an outside world," he said, adding that he spends much of his time away from Ottawa talking to service and consumer groups.
Part of that is accurate. However, what I actually said should be put on the record to show what I meant. I said, as recorded at page 5025 of Hansard:
It must be admitted that the press in the big cities does not do the job it should in telling the people of Canada what the score is, so I believe in taking the government to the people. I myself do it on Wednesday nights when this institution is not sitting, and I also do it on Friday evenings and on the weekends, so let no one say to me that I am jeopardizing my job here. I work seven days a week, and that is my business if I want to make that sacrifice on behalf of the people of Canada.
It has also been reported in several other newspapers, as intimated in telephone calls I received over the weekend, that I said members of the opposition were damn liars. One headline reads, "Criticism just 'damn lies'". I spoke when Your Honour's assistant was in the chair. I talked about consultation, and so on, with members of other departments concerned, and about consumer and producer concerns. I said, and I quote:
I see nothing wrong with departments that are concerned about trade and all these other things working together and coming to a mutual understanding on what we are trying to do about food production in this country. I have been accused of being just a representative of the farmers. That is a damn lie, and I will say so at mass on Sunday if anybody wants me to do that. It is a damn lie, because if I can make a strong agricultural industry, all society benefits, not just agriculture
If what I said had been reported accurately, there would be a better understanding, which would be better for all of us. What I said may have been reported, but if it was, it was not recorded in the press.

subsubtopic: ADVERSE EFFECTS OF MARIJUANA
speechtext:
1.	Is the government aware of the increasing availability of new information on the adverse effects of marijuana smoking and, if so, for what reason is the Department of National Health and Welfare not making this known to the youth of this country?
2.	Is the government aware of a recent study by Dr. Masters and his team (April 16,1974-New England Journal of Medicine) and, if so, is the

Minister prepared to publicize the results of that finding which indicated a forty per cent reduction in the body's protection against disease in a once-a-week user of marijuana over a year, as well as reports of serious chromosome breakage in sixty per cent of those using marijuana once a week?
3.	Does the government intend to publicize the results of the January 1974 issue of the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology dealing with chromosome breakage in marijuana users?
4.	Is the government planning any kind of a national advertising campaign, particularly in light of new findings to make known the harmful effects of marijuana smoking?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: ADVERSE EFFECTS OF MARIJUANA
speechtext:
1. The government is fully aware of all new information regarding cannabis from Canada, the United States and other countries. In general, these findings have confirmed earlier evidence that cannabis has a number of complex effects on the human body after smoking or ingestion. These effects are both physical and psychological in nature. A large amount of conformatory and analytic research is presently underway in both Canada and abroad relating to the significance of these effects in terms of their potential hazards for public health and society as a whole. It should be noted that there is a wide discrepancy at this time between the conclusions of various researchers partly because of the difficulty that has been experienced in carrying out animal research with cannabis, and partly because of the greatly varying strengths available in one country as compared to another.
2.	There have been reports of an effect of cannabis on the reproductive cells of some animal species but not present evidence of any lasting effect in humans. There is no evidence that the children born to parents who utilize cannabis have an increased incidence of congenital deformities and no child born of a cannabis-using mother has demonstrated cannabis addiction after birth. The recent communication of Drs. Kolodny and Masters reported that sex hormone levels in cannabis users was approximately 40 per cent less than levels found in control persons who do not use cannabis in any form. It should be added that cessation from marijuana use for a period of two weeks resulted in a return to complete normalcy. A recent verbal report soon to be published has failed to confirm the findings of Kolodny and Masters. The disparity may be explained by the fact that most cannabis users also employ other drugs some of which by themselves depress sex hormone levels. The work which has been carried out regarding the effect of cannabis on immunity is based on laboratory evidence only and refers to the ability of certain white blood cells called lymphocytes to react to a chemical form of stimulation. The precentage changes in function cannot be readily extrapolated to the clinical situation where cannabis is metabolized into many derivatives during the time that it is circulating in the body and coming into contact with specific organs and cells.
3.	The study of Dr. Morton Stenchever was published in the January issue of the "American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology". It is available for any media to publicize further.
4.	The government will continue to make information available that will keep the Canadian population aware of the effects of various psychotropic substances including cannabis (marijuana).

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the right hon. Prime Minister who will be aware that since he left these shores there has been a substantial number of charges laid in connection with dredging contracts, the basis of which is a massive fraud. Since these charges arose out of an investigation requested by the Solicitor General, who would have received progress reports from time to time as the investigation proceeded, would the Prime Minister tell the House approximately when he was first informed by the Solicitor General of the possibility of such a massive fraud, as has now been reinforced by the charges that have been laid?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: DREDGING CONTRACTS-WHEN PRIME MINISTER FIRST AWARE OF POSSIBILITY OF FRAUD-POSSIBLE INVESTIGATION OF PROCEDURE FOR LETTING CONTRACTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, subject to checking my memory and my files, I would say that my knowledge of such events from the Solicitor General was quite recent. He did talk to me in my office about the SIU series of events, but I cannot remember that dredging was brought into the discussion at that point.

subsubtopic: DREDGING CONTRACTS-WHEN PRIME MINISTER FIRST AWARE OF POSSIBILITY OF FRAUD-POSSIBLE INVESTIGATION OF PROCEDURE FOR LETTING CONTRACTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, has the Prime Minister caused any investigation to be conducted directly under his own order or direction into the procedures followed by his government with regard to the letting of contracts for dredging, and the supervising of the letting of such contracts, in order to satisfy himself that the procedure followed was proper?

subsubtopic: DREDGING CONTRACTS-WHEN PRIME MINISTER FIRST AWARE OF POSSIBILITY OF FRAUD-POSSIBLE INVESTIGATION OF PROCEDURE FOR LETTING CONTRACTS
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. When I first heard about the possibility of misconduct in that area I did discuss it with the Minister of Transport to ensure myself that he was looking into the files to assure himself that everything had been correctly performed as far as the department was concerned.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the scope of the charges and the possible extent of the conspiracy and fraud here on a national scale, and I emphasize that word "possible"


Oral Questions
because nothing is fact until it is proven, does the Prime Minister really feel he is satisfied in discharging his duties as Prime Minister in pursuing what seems to be a very casual approach to such a possible massive fraud, and can he not assure the House that in the interest of reassuring the Canadian public and reaffirming the good name and openness of his government throughout the country that he will sponsor a public inquiry?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know to whom or to what the Leader of the Opposition is referring when he mentions a casual approach. Surely, the fact that charges have been laid, verdicts of guilty have already been rendered and the extent to which this inquiry has been conducted and charges laid would seem to prove to the contrary, that neither the police nor the government have been lax or have taken a casual approach to this whole matter. I forget the second part of the question.
A public inquiry.

At this stage, Mr. Speaker, I have given the matter some thought; I understand it was brought up during my absence. I must say that my conclusions are the same as those stated by the Acting Prime Minister. The progress in the case, the actions of the police at the various levels, the system of justice under which we operate and under which several individuals are now to undergo trial, and the fact that no allegations have been made by the opposition nor by anyone else, are of a nature to show we should not depart from the normal process of criminal justice which exists in Canada and resort to what I have referred to before as an inquisitorial system of justice where you go on fishing expeditions against people who are the subject of no accusation. As a Liberal Government-and I believe this is also the mood of the people and corresponds to the system of justice in our country today-we do not inquire into people unless there is real cause to believe the normal process of ordinary justice is being subverted.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition on a final supplementary.

Mr. Speaker, it is not clear to me to what institution the Leader of the Opposition is referring in his last sentence-
The Government of Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Prime Minister. In raising the question I want also to assure the Prime Minister that we in our party want to avoid an inquisitorial approach to this question.

subtopic: DREDGING CONTRACTS-GOVERNMENT VIEW OF NEED FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY RATHER THAN CHARGES UNDER CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: DREDGING CONTRACTS-GOVERNMENT VIEW OF NEED FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY RATHER THAN CHARGES UNDER CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext: It is for that reason that I wish to put the following question to the Prime Minister. In view of the broadness of scope of the Inquiries Act, which is on the statute books of Canada, and the narrowness of scope of the Criminal Code, and in view of the broadness of the connections of the men who have been charged, not only with other companies which have contracts with other government departments but have contracts at senior levels with the governing party in Canada, is it the Prime Minister's view that public confidence in the institution of democratic politics and, more particularly, in the institution of this parliament, can be maintained through an inquiry that will take place exclusively within the framework of the Criminal Code of Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: DREDGING CONTRACTS-GOVERNMENT VIEW OF NEED FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY RATHER THAN CHARGES UNDER CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext: The short answer to that is yes, Mr. Speaker. It is true that that confidence must be maintained, and the answer is yes, full stop. I was going on to say that it is true that the Inquiries Act does have a much broader scope and this government has not hesitated to use that scope, for instance, in setting up boards to investigate prices and the Berger commission. That type of action is very much in line with the government's approach when it is useful to shed full light on objective facts. But when we get into the area of possible misbehaviour, and areas which relate to the integrity of individual Canadians, our approach is quite the opposite. I think that the law makers of this country, and indeed of Great Britain, who set the pattern for the criminal justice which we practice, were very conscious of the fact that they were making the scope of the Criminal Code narrow because they wanted the burden of proof not to lie with the defendant but with the state, and that is our approach.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a question to the right hon. Prime Minister whom I welcome to Parliament upon his return from a trip to Europe.
During his stay in Europe, while he was visiting five or six countries of the European Economic Community to find markets for Canadian trade, the economic situation here did not improve, unemployment and prices continued to rise. speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED MEETING BETWEEN PRIME MINISTER AND ORGANIZATIONS ON MEASURES TO FIGHT INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I should like to thank the hon. member for his kind words of welcome. May I point out to him that I chose to come back on St. Patrick's Day and that it took an Irishman like to him to welcome me back upon my return.
As to his question, may I reassure the hon. member by telling him that the type of contacts he suggests have already been made in many ways. The Minister of Finance and other ministers have had the opportunity of meeting several representatives of various organizations. The cabinet as such was also given the advice and suggestions of the Chamber of Commerce quite recently; we are to meet the Canada Labour Council very soon.
On a higher level, Mr. Speaker, I would remind the hon. member that the federal government has invited the provincial governments to a federal-provincial conference on the economy to be held right after Easter.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a supplementary question to the Prime Minister.
As a result of his trip in Europe which we have closely followed, does the government leader feel that the European situation is such that the Canadian people must necessarily be punished on the pretext that this is an international issue and that our country is almost helpless? Does the Prime Minister not think that, without being prejudicial to other countries, Canada can surely manage to act according to its own decisions, irrespective of what is going on in European countries?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED MEETING BETWEEN PRIME MINISTER AND ORGANIZATIONS ON MEASURES TO FIGHT INFLATION

This is perhaps why, according to the OECD statistics, the economic performance of Canada in 1974 was the best of all industrialized countries. The countries which I visited did not fail to congratulate us for it.

speechtext:
That the	House of Commons approve the government's
program of guideline dates for metric conversion;
And that a message be sent to the Senate informing Their Honours that this House has adopted a resolution approving a program of guideline dates for metric conversion, and requesting Their Honours to unite with this House in the approval of the same by filling up the blanks in the resolution with the words "Senate and".
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am speaking today on a matter that is fundamental to the long-term health and prosperity of the Canadian economy-the metric system of weights and measures. It is my pleasure to introduce to parliament today a joint resolution for a program of guideline dates for metric conversion in Canada. Some members may recall that I mentioned on March 11 last year that the government intended to introduce such a resolution.
In taking this step, the government wants to emphasize the importance of reaching a national consensus on the objective of a metric Canada by the decade of the 1980s. When my predecessor tabled in this House the white paper on metric conversion in January of 1970, a little over five years ago, it received the support of all party leaders. The federal government then launched the national metric conversion program through establishment by order in council in June of 1971 of the Metric Commission. Much has been accomplished and is being accomplished by this commission. Commission members have consulted and collaborated with national industry associations, consum-


Metric Conversion
er groups, unions, professional bodies and provincial and federal government departments.
They have begun a process of continuing investigation, planning, scheduling and implementation. Some 200 organizations in all parts of Canada are taking part in this metric conversion program which stems from the first meeting of the Metric Commission in January of 1972. The 18 metric commissioners appointed by the cabinet have enlisted nearly 1,000 persons from all sectors of the Canadian economy. These people have volunteered to serve on steering and sector committees which report to the Metric Commission. They are contributing their expert knowledge and professional skills to this important program. Their work in the investigation phase is now leading to integrated plans to transform their sectors from a measurement system which has now been abandoned by all but a very few nations of the world to one which is universally recognized, the International System of Units, SI.
The program of guideline dates which I will describe has the unanimous support of this nationwide committee structure and of the governments of all the provinces. Canada is joining the other members of the Englishspeaking world now converting and other major trading nations which are already metric in the use of this common and convenient measuring system.
Our most important trading partner, the United States, is also moving in this direction. Although in the last Congress metric legislation in the House of Representatives was set aside on a procedural question, Congress did authorize expenditure of $10 million a year for four years for metric education in schools. In this session Congress specifically recognized the increasing use of metric measures in the United States and the fact that these measures would inevitably become the dominant system of weights and measures in that country.
In the present Congress bills to implement the recommendation of the U.S. metric report have already been submitted. A bill sponsored by the administration and designed to appease objections raised by labour and small business is ready to be put forward. There is reasonable confidence that such a bill can be passed before adjournment in August of the present session of Congress. In the meantime, many major companies in the United States have embarked on programs for metric conversion. These programs are going forward without reference to action, or lack of action, in Congress.
To co-ordinate this development in industry, the United States has established the American National Metric Council. This council has more than 1,300 subscribers drawn from industries, association and individuals and expects to double its membership this year. A widespread committee structure has been established and there is frequent communication at all levels between the Metric Commission organization here in Canada and the American National Metric Council. Discussions have also been held with executive departments and agencies of the U.S. federal government. They are anxious to know of the Canadian plans in their areas of responsibility. Every effort will be made to co-ordinate work between the two

countries so as to obtain the greatest benefits for the Canadian program.
To develop an economy in which the use of the International System of Units is normal procedure, the Metric Commission has recommended, and the government has approved, a four phase program. These phases are: first, investigation-to determine what needs to be done; second, planning-to identify the sequence of activities and the relationships among things to be accomplished; third, scheduling-to assign specific target dates to planned events and to co-ordinate these between and among sectors; fourth, implementation-during which the actions to be performed are carried out as planned and according to schedule.
The following guideline dates for metric conversion in Canada which I propose for the approval of the House today correspond to the four major phases I have just mentioned. The investigation phase is now essentially completed. The remaining program dates are therefore proposed as follows: the planning phase, which began in 1973, is to extend through this year; the scheduling phase is to be completed in 1976; the implementation phase, which we expect to become significant this year, will reach a peak of activity by the years 1977 and 1978-it should be substantially completed by the end of 1980, at which time metric measures will be used by all Canadians for all normal commercial and legal purposes.
We shall be organizing three pilot projects in retail store conversion. The cities of Sherbrooke, Quebec, Peterborough, Ontario, and Kamloops, British Columbia, will pioneer metric, probably in 1978. All retail store scales will be changed to metric in those cities at that time. Meanwhile, many products will appear on the shelves to be sold in metric quantities. I repeat that the guideline dates which I have just mentioned are the result of nationwide consultation with governments, industry, consumers and labour. With the approval of hon. members, they will constitute the basic framework for a national metric conversion program.
Many letters urging the adoption of this program have been received from national associations. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association, for instance, writes:
The association believes that the publication of these guidelines will be a useful encouragement to business to proceed with the planning and preparation needed for the proper integration of the conversion process.
From the Canadian Chamber of Commerce we hear:
The objective of completing substantially the conversion program by 1980 is a worth-while goal, considering the already wide international usage of the metric system and the pace of development of conversion in the United States.
The Canadian Federation of Retail Grocers writes:
We believe the commission's approach is a reasonable one and deserves all the support we can give it.
Both the Canadian Nurses' Association and the Association of Nurses of the province of Quebec have given their unqualified support to the guideline dates program, and the Canadian Office Products Association "finds the dates as outlined acceptable to all aspects of our industry." The Canada Grains Council has made public its scheme for the grains trade, and this conforms fully with the guideline dates I am proposing. The interests of the Canadian con-

sumer are being well represented by the Consumers Association of Canada which is taking an active interest in conversion plans. The association's influence has already resulted in some products now appearing in metric-size packaging.
We expect that consumers will gradually become accustomed to metric measures as products and services are increasingly made available in metric units. Already, weather reports on radio give temperatures in degrees Celsius, and from April of this year temperatures will be given in Celsius only. Rainfall in millimetres and snow in centimetres will follow, hopefully in another season.
The views I have quoted represent only a small sample of the support the metric system has received and is receiving. There is every indication that the vast majority of organizations in Canadian society are committed to the eventual use of the metric system and support the proposed program of guideline dates. Many Canadian firms have already begun investigating and planning for metric conversion. They are now awaiting parliamentary approval of these dates before synchronizing their schedules with others. In the public sector, federal government department and all provincial governments have created interdepartmental committees to co-ordinate metric conversion.
It is of the utmost importance that all Canadians move in concert to maintain the momentum of the four-phase program. To this end, an information program is now under way to explain the changes contemplated and the manner in which they will affect each one of us. During the coming year, increasing numbers of packaged goods will carry declarations of content in millilitres and litres, in grams and kilograms. By March, 1976, all pre-packaged goods will carry metric markings and many will be packed in metric sizes. Hon. members have already seen some road signs giving distances in kilometres. By September of 1977 it is expected that all across Canada we shall see road signs with distances in kilometers and permitted speeds in kilometres per hour. Already this year the speedometers on many automobiles are marked in kilometers per hour as well as the familiar miles per hour.
Canadians in the labour force will also be made aware of changes initiated in industry, commerce and public services. Suitable training programs are helping them to appreciate the simplicity and convenience of the metric system. In many schools the metric system is being taught at the elementary level as the basic system of measurement. Thus, young Canadians now at elementary schools will, on graduation from their secondary or university studies, be living and working with all other Canadians in a metric world.
Hon. members may be aware that a number of companies have already converted or are well along in the conversion process. For example, the Price Pulp and Paper Company of Newfoundland has moved to the production of newsprint on a metric basis. This mill produces exclusively for offshore markets and it has switched its whole operation, including billing and order forms, to metric. They experienced no significant problem in mill conversion.
Metric Conversion
The Steel Company of Canada has gone metric, too, in its new pipe mill at Welland, Ontario. The machinery of this mill is entirely metric and produces welded pipe to both inch-pound and metric specifications. The new steelmaking facilities being developed on the shores of Lake Erie at Nanticoke are being designed exclusively in metric terms and will be an entirely metric operation. At Varennes, Quebec, ASEA Limited, the big Swedish producer of heavy electrical equipment, had been producing entirely metric products, using local labour, for the past year. The working force was trained by the company and they have had no difficulty in maintaining efficient operation and production.
Metric conversion is not unique to Canada; it is nothing new. Canada will be drawing on the experience of Great Britain, South Africa and Australia in the conversion process. In Great Britain, for example, many large industries have converted. Experience has been generally favourable. As a matter of fact, in nearly all cases costs of conversion were very susbtantially lower than original estimates and difficulties in training the work force were minimal. Many British industries have achieved very substantial economies in production by using the opportunity of metric conversion to effect a rationalization and sim-plication of their operations. Some difficulties are currently being experienced in Britain due to delays in carrying through the program at the level of the ultimate consumer. This has resulted in a need to operate for an extended period in both systems.
The lack of a clear commitment in consumer related aspects of the U.K. program has probably been the major inhibiting factor. But these difficulties have been recognized by responsible officials in the United Kingdom and they are directing attention to ensuring that enabling legislation is passed in the consumer goods sector and that there is a broad-based commitment to the national program in both the private and public sectors.
In South Africa, the experience has been good. After a seven-year program of conversion, no significant difficulties have been experienced. Industries report that drawing office staffs, once they had worked in metric for a few weeks, would not go back to working in Imperial units. This is because of the greater simplicity of working in metric units and the relative freedom from error.
Australia is about two years ahead of Canada in conversion. Implementation is now in full swing. Much of agriculture has already been converted without any adverse reaction. All transport tariffs and customs and excise tariffs were placed on a metric basis last year. Some 50 per cent of grocery products on the shelves of Australian stores are now in metric-size packages. This has proved entirely acceptable to the consuming public. Speed limits and road distance signs were converted to metric units in May of 1973. The conversion was accomplished without a hitch.
Here in Canada, to draw attention to metric conversion the Metric Commission had developed a distinctive logo. It is promoting the use of this logo to identify Canadian products in metric size or design as well as texts or announcements making correct use of metric units and advertisements of Canadian metric products. During the past year the commission has approved a growing number

Metric Conversion
of applications from interests wishing to use this logo to identify their metric products. The commission expects use of the logo will become widespread and hopes to promote in the general public an immediate recognition of it as an indicator of metric conversion in Canada.
Undoubtedly metric conversion will involve costs. However, these costs will be spread over a period of time as industries proceed to implementation of their plans. As I have said, implementation is not expected to reach its peak until 1977-78 and will be spread over a period of years. Concern has also been expressed that the cost of conversion might impose an undue hardship on some small businesses. In view of this concern, the cabinet has approved a program of loans and loan guarantees to be available to small businesses, to be called the small business metric conversion assistance program. These loans would cover specific eligible costs of metric conversion by small businesses. In this context, small business will include farming and fishing enterprises. Such loan assistance would be available to businesses facing special financing difficulties resulting from metric conversion when such businesses were unable to obtain financing from commercial lending institutions. I expect the federal Business Development Bank to play the main role in this assistance plan for small enterprises.
My department, working in co-operation with the Treasury Board and the Department of Finance, is developing detailed criteria and administrative procedures for this program. However, we must keep in mind that costs of conversion are one-time costs while the benefits of conversion are continuing. They will be apparent in increased trade opportunities and in efficiencies which will result from standardization and rationalization. I cannot say too strongly that any delay in the program of metric conversion will only postpone realization of benefits and increase costs. Every instrument or device now being designed to Imperial units is a further liability for eventual cost of conversion.
What about information on this program, Mr. Speaker? Where can the ordinary Canadian find out what is going to happen? The information is being and will continue to be disseminated through the ten regional offices of my department and through the regional offices of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Furthermore, metric information will be disseminated by the federal Business Development Bank when it starts operation. We are also receiving excellent co-operation from the provinces and each province will have a metric co-ordinator.
I have been assured that these offices can cope with present and anticipated inquiries concerning metric conversion. The commission has produced many booklets and films. To help tell the metric story, there is also a speaker's bureau and more than 50 seminars have already been held in cities and centres across Canada. A series of seminars called "Metric and You" is currently being conducted by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and the Metric Commission in co-operation with local chambers of commerce and provincial chambers. Hon. members will recall that when the white paper on metric conversion was tabled in this House in January of 1970 there was unanimous support for the principle that metric conversion is not only inevitable but in the national interest.

The legal basis for using the metric or decimal system was first introduced in the Weights and Measures Act of 1873. This was reaffirmed and brought up to date with the incorporation of SI-the simplest and most modern version of the metric system-in the Weights and Measures Act passed by this House in April of 1971, 98 years later.
Against this background, I ask all hon. members for their approval of the guideline dates which I have outlined. This will ensure that Canada keeps pace with an already largely metric world. This program is the subject of the resolution that I now place before the House. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, under Standing Order 41(2) I should like to table, in both official languages, a statement entitled "Program of guideline dates for metric conversion".

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE PROGRAM OF GUIDELINE DATES FOR METRIC CONVERSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to lead off this debate for the official opposition and put forth our position in the clearest possible terms on metric conversion in Canada. The motion presented on the order paper in the name of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) simply states that the House of Commons approves the government's program of guideline dates for metric conversion, and there follows the usual reference to the other place. The minister has set forth the schedule and has asked us to concur.
I think I should say at the outset that we supported metric conversion when it was introduced by order in council and the white paper, and that is our position today: we still support it, but we have reservations and I hope to place them on the record during this debate. I hope the minister will take note of them and see that something specific is done about them.
Since order in council PC-1971-1145 of June 10, 1971, was passed we have been approving sums of money in the estimates for the metric conversion fund and by the end of this fiscal year the commission will have spent over $7 million. We must ask ourselves what value we have received for the $7 million that will be spent by the end of this fiscal year.
Let me say again that we in the official opposition support the principle of metric conversion. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) stated our position which appears in Hansard of July 16, 1970, at page 2470. He gave our support to the principle of metric conversion. The hon. member for Peace River also mentioned the fact that


the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean) had in 1970 put forward a private member's bill calling for a metric system inquiry commission. He also stated that the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), when he was prime minister, had his ministers undertake studies in this field.
I have taken this opportunity to record again the fact that the official opposition has had a keen interest in the metric system for a number of years. We supported the principle in 1970 and we support the principle of metric conversion today. Having said that, we do not intend to let the matter pass without recording in this House our dissatisfaction with the progress made by the Metric Commission. We want to bring into perspective the position of the Metric Commission today, in 1975, and let the minister know in the strongest possible terms that we are appalled at the lack of progress being made.
I stated that by the end of this fiscal year the Metric Commission will have spent over $7 million. Since 1970 it has produced one annual report and has promised a second report by late 1975. That is atrocious when we consider the amount of money the commission is spending. The commission has not appeared before a standing committee of this House; it has not justified its program, its progress or its expenditures. I know that some members opposite will say we have an opportunity during the consideration of estimates to examine the work of the Metric Commission, but that is a lot of nonsense. We all know how the standing committees are structured and that we have little time under the rules of the House to examine in depth the Metric Commission's program.
The first time I met anyone from the Metric Commission was at a dinner party in the parliamentary diningroom, I think in 1973. Members of the commission brought along a few slides and a projector to put forward a public relations package. One of the slides they put on the screen was a map of Canada which showed that the capital of Manitoba was Edmonton and the capital of Alberta was Winnipeg. Can you imagine anyone coming before a group of parliamentarians and showing a map of Canada that contained such errors? It was incredible, but I think it is also typical of the way the commission operates.
Because of our close ties with the United States, we feel we must phase in our metric conversion with theirs. The minister has said there is a measure of co-operation in respect of lyur metric commission and that of the United States, but I do not think this co-operation is as strong as it might be. From our investigations, United States industry is progressing much faster than Canadian industry in spite of the fact that no legislation is in place at this moment in the United States.
There are problems in respect of road signs and odometers in automobiles to be worked out, to which the minister made reference in his remarks. There is little co-ordination between the provinces and the federal government, in spite of what the minister had to say. Another problem which we have can be related to the considerable amount of across the border travel that takes place. It is imperative, in our view, that we work closely with the United States government and individual state authorities, many of which have metric programs under way, in order to
Metric Conversion
ensure the least possible confusion in the conversion of road signs.
I now want to say a few words about the Metric Commission and its operation. We have spoken to numerous people involved with the Metric Commission, and the general impression we get is that the commission is engaged, basically, in a public relations job. Apparently there is much indecision, lack of leadership and, generally speaking, poor morale. We note that the commission has had considerable staff turnover at all levels. It is our belief that the commission has serious internal problems which stem generally from lack of direction and indecision.
Let us consider the question of conversion, in respect of weather reporting, from Fahrenheit to Celsius. I understand this program was ready to go last summer and a booklet was supposed to have been prepared that should have found its way into the school system last September in order to take advantage of the splash-over effect from students to parents. The date of April 1 was set for the changeover, but on January 13 nothing had really been done: the program was still sitting on the director's desk and the opportunity of using the school system was lost. We understand there was then an attempt to put off the April 1 conversion date and to substitute a later date.
As I say, this is an example of the indecision and lack of direction that permeates the Metric Commission. Many of the commissioners appointed were political appointments, and the director of the Metric Commission suffers from a political appointment without political support. When was the last time hon. members heard any minister of the Crown mention anything about metric conversion? Have we heard any minister mention anything about it? Have we read any ministers' speeches which have contained anything about metric conversion? To my knowledge, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has never made any mention of metric conversion in any of his speeches. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) had two opportunities recently, when he spoke to the Consumers Association of Canada and to the Canadian Construction Association, to mention metric conversion; but not a word was said.
The Consumers Association of Canada, which the minister says is co-operating with the commission, has registered some very serious concerns about metric conversion, but as I understand it the association has received no assurance that its views will be heeded. Let me read a few comments from a letter sent by the association to the minister on January 7, 1975. The association writes:
Participants from our association advise me that at the present time there is a substantial degree of dissatisfaction, and poor morale, within all the sectors of the commission's work in which programs are supposed to be developed for the information and assistance of such final users. It would appear, accordingly, that an early decision on your part to request a comprehensive review of procedures and programs in these areas would be advisable, and would certainly be well received by our own participants, and would, as I am advised, also be well received and receive the co-operation of other participants in these areas.
The letter goes on to state that the Consumers Association of Canada would be prepared to meet with the minister or his officials at any time to discuss these issues and to provide specific examples of policies and procedures


Metric Conversion
which concern them at the moment. This letter, in essence, is saying that the Consumers Association in fact would just as soon pull out of the program, but does not suggest doing that and wishes to make a contribution to it. This is a very interesting letter. So far as I am aware, this association has had no reply from the minister about its concerns.
We have been told that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs will monitor the packaging industry and retail stores to ensure that the consumer is not the loser. We have had the experience of the British metric conversion where there was evidence that the packaging and retail trades took the opportunity during the conversion to adjust prices upward while at the same time reducing, in some instances, the quantity.
We are not convinced that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs will be in any way effective in this matter. We have received no reports in this House, so far as I am aware, that there has been any monitoring in respect of other government programs. On several occasions members have put questions to the ministers, the reply has been that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs will monitor the programs; however, we have not heard anything about this monitoring. I wonder whether it is a dodge used by the government to assure consumers that Big Brother is looking after their best interests.
I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the members of the official opposition will very carefully watch this monitoring. We want to be sure that the experience of Britain is not duplicated in this country. We should not be proceeding by order in council or by resolution; we should be proceeding by means of a bill.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE PROGRAM OF GUIDELINE DATES FOR METRIC CONVERSION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE PROGRAM OF GUIDELINE DATES FOR METRIC CONVERSION
speechtext:
We should have a bill which sets out all the details of the program. The guidelines and the program should be laid down so that we may proceed in an orderly fashion. Instead, we have a loosely worded order in council which allows the Metric Commission to proceed as it sees fit. I believe it would have been better to have a bill, to have a full debate and then to have the Metric Commission appear before a committee and reappear each year to justify its program and expenditures. We see in this commission another government body removed from the scrutiny of parliament. We see it as a group that is a law unto itself and which proceeds as it sees fit.
I talked to officials of the commission about the terms of reference in the order in council. I was appalled by their reply. I noted that in paragraph 7 it states that the commission shall advise the minister on the need for legislation or any other action that may be required to facilitate conversion to the metric system. I asked whether they intended to advise the minister that legislation is necessary, and how they intended to proceed. The reply was that they intended to follow the wording which says "or any other action". In other words, they do not want a bill or guidelines; they want to be a law unto themselves so they make their own rules and proceed as they see fit. I have the feeling that we should have the Auditor General review their spending and have them appear before the public accounts committee to justify their spending.
fMr. Kempling.]
Numerous groups have registered their dissatisfaction with the progress of the commission. The proposition of "let the costs fall where they may" is surely the height of folly. As things stand at the moment, lack of leadership at the federal level has led to confusion on the part of the public. Industry is waiting and watching for someone else to make the move.
In respect of what the minister said about the provinces having programs, I checked with every province and find that none has a cabinet policy or a stable program concerning metric conversion. They are all waiting for direction from the minister. It may seem to many that the idea of letting the costs fall where they may is the cheapest way to do it, but the sector committees have no authority; they are neither paid nor reimbursed for their expenses. As a consequence, there is a high turnover. If this matter were not so vital to industry perhaps it would be all right to let the costs fall where they may.
I have the impression that the Metric Commission believes that by a snap of the finger we will be metric by 1980. Nothing could be further from the truth. There is good and bad news in these remarks, so having said what I have, may I say that I welcome the minister's statement to the effect that he will introduce a program under the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce to assist small business. I commend him for that. I think assistance in metric conversion will be well received by small business. I think the offer of assistance by the federal Business Development Bank to help them in their financing is fine, but we want the minister to go a little further.
If we can finance export development trade at 7 per cent interest and give loans to Cuba at 3 per cent, why can we not have a special rate, say a prime rate, that would be used specifically in respect of metric conversion? As the minister has said, this is a far reaching program which will affect every industry in the country. If we can finance programs outside the country at rates of 3 per cent and 7 per cent, surely to goodness we can do something inside the country at a special rate. I hope the minister will take a serious look at this matter.
The beverage industry in Canada has a particular problem. From my discussions with that industry it would seem that it is making pretty good progress in its conversion, although there is a particular problem. The industry has $40 million worth of re-usable bottles which have an average life of ten years. The industry is awaiting clearance of double labelling by volume so it can use the $40 million worth of bottles. I am told that it would take six to seven years to carry out the complete conversion. We are five years down the road now, so there is no way this conversion will be completed by 1978 or 1980.
Automobile mechanics have a problem in securing new tools. Some modification must be made concerning the tool allowance under the Income Tax Act. I hope the minister will speak to his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), and suggest that in the next budget provision be made to increase the $150 tool allowance for automobile mechanics. The industry which stands to make the greatest gain from metric conversion is the construction industry. It stands to gain by way of cost reduction under metric conversion. Standardization of building components should be encouraged, yet the Minister of Public

Works (Mr. Drury) has taken no initiative in respect of metric conversion with respect to public buildings. Nothing has been said in any of his speeches about metric conversion. The same thing applies to the remainder of the cabinet; they have all been quiet on the subject.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE PROGRAM OF GUIDELINE DATES FOR METRIC CONVERSION
speechtext: How about dredging?

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE PROGRAM OF GUIDELINE DATES FOR METRIC CONVERSION
speechtext:
I do not know whether dredging will be done under the metric system, but this is an area which might be worth looking into. The provinces and the municipalities are waiting for initiative on the part of the Minister of Public Works. When will we see it? If you look at the total of the buildings which the Department of Public Works erects in the course of a year, and add to it provincial and municipal undertakings, you will find that it represents a large portion of the construction in this country. Surely the department should show some initiative and give some leadership to the provinces and municipalities which await government action in this area because they are aware of the advantages of metric conversion.
I should like to sum up what I have said. We support the Metric Commission. We want to see it act in co-operation with our neighbour to the south. However, we are very concerned about the operation of the Metric Commission. We believe that it needs a good shake-up, that it needs firm direction and that it needs support from the minister and from other members of the cabinet. We believe that the structure of the sector committees must be given careful consideration. If they are not functioning properly, they should be reconstituted. The committee must have some authority; and we are not sure that the use of volunteer help is the best way to proceed. As I understand it, sector committees sit about four times a year. Committee members come to Ottawa at their own expense. I think some provision is made to cover travel costs if they travel beyond Winnipeg, in which case I believe they get 25 per cent of the fare but no per diem. While this may be economical, I do not think the best results can be obtained from employing volunteer help, because they have no authority.
Metric conversion in Canada will put us in step with the rest of the world. As I read recently in a magazine, the People's Republic of Yemen, Burma, Canada and the United States are the only countries in the world not on the metric system. Metric conversion must go forward and for this we must have leadership and direction, both of which we lack at present. We look to the minister to give the commission a good swift boot to get them in line and get this program under way.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE PROGRAM OF GUIDELINE DATES FOR METRIC CONVERSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate in the debate this afternoon but I am sorry to hear that we are not more advanced in converting to the metric system, as is apparent from the timetable outlined by the minister. In looking in my file I find that in 1968 I introduced a bill regarding metric conversion. The bill is designed to provide a technique of study for the applicability to Canada of the metric system. The appointment of a commission of senior public servants is intended, first to avoid the costs and delays inherent in the
Metric Conversion
appointment of a royal commission, and second to ensure the completion of studies and reports within a reasonable period of time. I have been wondering, since I looked this up, why I have become so interested in the whole matter of metric conversion since I do not know very much about the subject. However, I am very interested in the history of the metric system as it was outlined by the previous speaker.
I understand that the Conservative government under the leadership of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) had undertaken a study within the government. Since nothing resulted from that study, it might seem that I should be given credit for what the government did, because on reading the bill one finds that the government followed my recommendations; so it seems as if I had written the program. This does not always happen. It is interesting to look back to the correspondence and see what one of the groups which wrote to me said at that time. I am referring to a letter which I received from the Canadian Teachers' Federation in which they said the federation had taken note of the bill respecting conversion to the metric system, and they put forward the following resolution:
The Canadian Teachers' Federation has taken note of Bill C-85 (an act respecting the metric system) which you had originally introduced in the House. We thought you might be interested in knowing that the Canadian Teachers' Federation has passed the following resolution:
"That the CTF encourage conversion to the metric system".
In 1970 I received a letter from the Canadian Institute of Quantity Surveyors after I introduced another bill in 1969. They wrote:
This letter is prompted by Bill C-42, designed to provide a technique of study for the applicability to Canada of the metric system, which you introduced to the House of Commons on October 30th last.
They went on to say they were of the following opinion:
(a)	Canadian conversion to the metric system must arise from economic necessity.
(b)	The desire to convert must be voluntarily generated by industry, and not by government.
(c)	Most importantly, to be effective the conversion must have the support of all levels of government, federal, provincial and municipal, and must permeate the entire national economy.
I also received a letter at that time from a gentleman who was very interested in the subject. He wrote:
If your bill is adopted, it could reasonably be expected that the commission would report in favour of the metric system. The presentation of the subject to the House of Commons, following the introduction of the report of the commission, would require a more comprehensive study of the wider implications of the question, nationally and internationally. I hope that a complete acceptance of units of the metric system for all uses in government, industry, commerce and merchandising would be possible, at the one time.
He went on to state some other advantages of the metric system. This was appreciated because, as I said, I am not an expert on the subject. When I introduced that bill I was familiar with a couple of problems that had developed and had been dealt with in parliament shortly before that time. While I certainly do not have the advantage of the knowledge possessed by the minister on this subject, I am particularly interested in an inquiry we undertook on the subject of conversion to the metric system of certain machinery and tools. At that time a great number of systems were being used in Canada for the measurement

Metric Conversion
of simple things like nuts and bolts and machine threads. There were right-hand threads, left-hand threads, and some bastardized sizes that did not fit anywhere.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE PROGRAM OF GUIDELINE DATES FOR METRIC CONVERSION
speechtext: It is always members of the NDP who make such statements.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE PROGRAM OF GUIDELINE DATES FOR METRIC CONVERSION
speechtext:
If the hon. member is referring to the word I used, there is a type of thread that goes by that name; but a member of parliament from the medical profession would probably not be familiar with that. His relationship with that word would be in another context.
It was obvious at that time that great advantage was to be gained from conversion to the metric system even in such a small area as the manufacture of nuts and bolts, so that a farmer would not have to choose from such a large selection of nuts and bolts for every farm implement. The other advantage would be derived from the fact that since tools for farm machinery come in all sizes, if we could adopt one universal system of measurement many units would become interchangeable and this would prove to be economical.
Whether or not these advantages are sufficiently great to warrant plunging the country into the cost and effort of metric conversion, with all it entails, is not clear. Since that time I have received a letter from the Teachers' Federation which points out that they have reconsidered the problem and are now prepared to act upon it. There again, they are having extreme difficulties because if they are going to act on it they will have to do so in a very heavy-handed way. They are of the opinion that they should go into the metric system fully and be prepared to teach it, not in comparison to the old system but as a new system and teach that and that only.
There are tables and other paraphernalia to allow for conversion factors. It is quite possible that the old system of feet, inches, chains and rods, pounds and all the other things common to the English measuring system should probably be taught in history now, because it is a very interesting subject and it would be interesting f on young people to find out how we, in a very archaic way, have developed our systems of measurement.
I agree that if we are going to convert, it has to be done fairly suddenly. I drove down Highway 11 in Ontario a few months ago and saw a sign which read 350 or 370 kilometres to Toronto. I wondered how far it was from North Bay to Toronto. I went down the road about half a mile and saw a sign which said it was 217 miles to Toronto.
I do not think the 217 miles should be translated into kilometres. The process of translating brings about many difficulties.
I would have liked the minister to explain a number of difficulties, which he did not mention, in the flow of this conversion to what is called the International System of Units. The International System of Units, as I understand it, is really what we call the metric system. It is a subject that was studied very carefully; this may account for the spending of some of the $7 million that we have heard about. I knew one of the senior officials-I met him socially quite regularly-and he was either going to, or coming from, Europe all the time.

speechtext: He must have been the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE PROGRAM OF GUIDELINE DATES FOR METRIC CONVERSION
speechtext:
I did not discuss it at any great length, but I understand they were discussing in a number of countries how they would make this conversion-even in countries which we thought were on the metric system previously, such as France and Italy. These countries are also having a great deal of difficulty in converting.
We would expect, when we listen to the weather announcements, to hear that it is two degrees centigrade or minus two degrees centigrade, but that is not what we hear: it is referred to as two degrees Celsius. I ask, what the hell is Celsius?
Of course, there are a number of temperature systems. There is a system with the absolute-that is a scientific scale-there is the Fahrenheit scale and there is the centigrade scale. There are at least one or two more temperature scales. I assume that instead of using the centigrade scale we would go to one of these outlandish scales which have been developed. I understand that Celsius was a scientist who played around with units of temperature and was responsible for the development of the centigrade scale. We call the other one Fahrenheit: I do not know whether he was the person who developed it.
Instead of going to centigrade, we went to the Celsius scale. I think the minister should have explained how that fits into the SI units of metric conversion, because I think this causes concern to people thinking in terms of centigrade and we find it is not being called that at all. I wonder if the people who announce the weather are having fun. Sometimes they are; they throw the chalk into the air and quite often they miss and put the highs where the lows should be.
Other countries are having difficulty with the SI system as well. The Metric Monitor contains some very good information. It also contains much propaganda. I do not understand what Premier Robert Bourassa's kilometer zero monument was established for, or why it is on the front page, but it does say that Mr. Boire, the executive director of the commission, when travelling around found that in England they are experiencing slow progress and lack of a positive attitude toward the adoption of the SI metric system. The Metric Monitor also says:
The British Metrication Board feels that the delay in carrying through the program was piling up unnecessary costs in industry due to the continuing requirements for production and inventory maintenance in both systems.
This was pointed out by the previous speaker, and it reflects surveys by independent businessmen in the small business community. They are very concerned at having to carry double inventories in many of their commodities. The Metric Monitor goes on to say:
The failure to communicate with the consumer and the extension of the changeover period has increased confusion and consumer reaction against the change.
France: Metric units and SI symbols are generally being properly applied to signs and packages. In industry, there is general reluctance to give up old metric pressure units such as the kilogram per square centimetre and the bar, plus considerable opposition to using the newton rather than the kilogram force. Temperature is generally referred to as degree centigrade rather than degree Celsius. SI is exlcusively taught at all educational levels, but new metric units are generally frowned upon at the industrial operating level.


It goes on to talk about Italy and other countries and what they have done. I think it is to Canada's credit that this has been done. The government cannot take much credit for it, because credit must go to the civil servants who have become very involved with a number of private businessmen who have co-operated with the advisory commission to develop a scheme across the world that will upgrade the metric system in countries which have been on the system for a long time.
When this conversion takes places, it should be truly representative of weights and measures. I do not know how to translate volume and other measurements, but the whole system must progress so that we do not find ourselves using a metric system in this country which is not in use in other countries. If they continue to use centigrade degrees and we use degrees Celsius, and if they use kilograms and we use something else, we will be no better off than we were in the first place. Other countries have spent on metric conversion the sums of money which our commission has spent on it. The idea of converting is to use a standard of measurement which will be universally accepted and adopted.
Some funny things can happen when you convert. Let me tell the House a little story. A man went to a lumber dealer and asked to purchase six feet of two by four pine, dressed four sides. "I'm sorry," said the salesman, "but we no longer sell lumber by the foot-pound system; everything is sold by metric measurement." "Very well", said the customer, "give me two metres of two by four pine, dressed four sides." The salesman said, "I must disappoint you again, sir; our two by four pine is available only in lengths of 1.83 and 2.44 metres." The customer was a bit confused at these odd sizes and asked; "Why do you stock only odd-numbered lengths?" The salesman replied, "It's because it is all rounded off to the nearest foot."
That story shows what could happen and how hard it may be for some people to figure out measurements under the metric system. The mathematical calculations are beyond the ability of many Canadians and, frankly, I do not want to learn how to operate a small computer when doing my conversions. Let me refer hon. members to an article in the Toronto Star, by Ellen Roseman, entitled "Consumers must switch-and maybe fight." It reads:
A woman went to her florist recently to buy a dozen roses. The florist charged her for a dozen roses but only gave her ten.
"We're using the metric system now and this is a metric dozen," he explained.
Stories like this make government officials livid with rage. There's no such thing as a metric dozen, they say, but try telling that to an unscrupulous merchant who sees metric conversion as a profit-making bonanza.
As overseer of the switch, the Metric Commission in Ottawa is urging producers not to smuggle in price changes along with metric size changes.
It is also asking producers to make the new metric sizes larger, rather than holding the price steady and shrinking the package.
There are no penalties in law for merchants who make extra profit out of conversion. The Metric Commission is relying on moral suasion to keep them in line. It's using the 110,000 members of the Consumers Asssociation of Canada as watchdogs.
Metric Conversion
Still, "there are some consumers who feel that merchants are salivating for the time when Canada goes metric and they can gouge away," says George Mailhot, a sector manager with the Metric Commission.
"This hasn't been the experience of Australia and Great Britain when they converted. Sure there were isolated cases, but no excess rip-off."
As I suggested in 1968 converting to the metric system, I am happy to note that the government did not delay too long in following my advice. I must sound a warning which the government would do well to heed. If the conversion is to be successful, the government must introduce a bill which will stipulate standards of measurement. We all know that present measurements of length and volume must meet certain federal standards. Penalties are provided in cases where standards are not met. The government should stipulate standard metric measurements which people in business in this country and in other occupations must meet. As well, the suggested date, 1980, for the implementation of metric measurement is unrealistic. I do not think it can be done much before 1985, and I suspect the minister will be satisfied if the new standards are wholly adopted by the year 2000.
We must guard against abuse and provide penalties for gouging which may result directly from conversion. Without safeguards, Canadians will not know if they are being cheated. I have often seen women in grocery stores trying to figure out whether a can or package labelled in metric units is smaller or larger than an apparently similar sized can or package labelled in today's standard units of measurement. The new units of measurement may puzzle consumers and we must provide safeguards against abuse. The old slogan in the marketplace, "Let the buyer beware," still holds good. We have all heard of the butcher who puts his thumb on the scales to make the package seem heavier. We must make sure that rip-off artists do not keep their thumbs on the scale. To prevent abuse, legislation will be necessary.
Small businesses may need help with conversion, help which could be provided under a bill. If the conversion is to be completed in the stipulated period, help will be necessary. I suggest that the small entrepreneur, the small, independent businessman who can only convert at considerable cost in terms of increased overhead will need help. Assistance will have to be provided. Against that, however, there is considerable advantage which will accrue to the larger companies: they will receive greater benefit from the conversion. It will be an opportunity for them to upgrade their operations. If they are given some assistance, they will be able to upgrade and modernize their facilities. This will obviously result in the production of a larger number of goods. Where we are now limited to countries which have the same measuring system as ours, with the metric system we will be able to compete in world markets.
I would like to know how the minister intends to assist the communities of this nation. Somebody mentioned fire hydrants. How will a small community change over its fire hydrants?
