speechtext:
-that there is the law of averages and there are about 15 or 18 different sizes. It is quite safe to say that four or five municipalities within greater Ottawa have systems that are not interchangeable. I would be surprised if even their radio equipment were interchangeable, and it is a very small matter when it comes to changing crystals. However, someone has to buy and change them.
Conversion to the metric system will cost money. Changes will have to be made in the whole social field. The minister knows very well the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce will gain by this conversion. His department could make the transition a lot easier by providing grants in order to make the conversion. I would like to suggest that his department provide a factory to manufacture some of this equipment, but that might not be acceptable to this government.
Another weakness in the conversion is the lack of response we have had from many of the provincial governments. I have always been interested in the province of Quebec in terms of international measurements, signs, and so on. In Ontario, there are huge, bilingual signs to show there is a bump in the road. Quebec has always followed the international system of just having a picture. In that province it is not a matter of the language you speak; their signs can be understood by all. I am quite sure there will be much greater acceptance of the metric system in the province of Quebec than in many other provinces. Some provinces will have difficulty meeting the responsibility which will fall on their shoulders. If there has been a weakness in the committees established to study metric conversion, it has been the provincial governments. If the minister is at all serious about his deadlines, he will have to get the co-operation of the provinces. This will involve a lot more discussion with the provinces.
I have often said the federal government has a responsibility toward education. I sincerely believe it has a very large responsibility at the junior levels of education with regard to conversational French. If it has that responsibility, it should pay for it. This government has been extreme-
ly lax in providing equality of opportunity to learn a second language. If that is true, it is equally true with regard to providing educational facilities for training young people in the metric system. It will be necessary for our educational institutions to have some assistance in replacing their equipment at as early a date as possible if our young people are to learn the metric system. Added to the other expenses the school boards and educational facilities have to meet this year, it will not be possible to meet this commitment without help from this government. The Canadian Teachers' Federation are anxious to meet this commitment.
The minister introduced this motion in a lackadaisical manner. He referred to it as a joint Senate and House of Commons motion to do something that has not been spelled out. He did not even attach to the motion the timetable which he later tabled. If we do not meet some of the problems I have referred to, it will not be possible for Canada to be on the metric system by 1980. In five years we have developed a lot of fancy documents. This booklet is a good example, and it has been duplicated by the dozen. More material is being turned out than one can imagine. On every page there is listed a different date by which the government expects conversion to take place. For example, it states:
Most provinces in Canada will be teaching metric as of September, 1974. Many provinces have run metric workshops for their teachers.
If they have not done so by now, they are not going to do it. It is now 1975 and we should know whether all schools are now teaching this system. As I stated, on each page of this booklet there is a different date for conversion. Under the heading "Shopping" it is said the conversion with regard to toothpaste would take place in 1973. Each page covers a different item and has a different date. For instance, talking about textiles they say:
Textiles will be dual-labelled for a time and then labelled in widths measured in centimetres and sold by the metre, probably by March,
1977.
Each page gives a different date by which these things are expected to take effect. Mr. Speaker, we cannot hope for much from a Liberal government. They never move very fast or very firmly. I give them full credit for having got this far. It surprises the hell out of me to find them accepting an idea which I thought was a very progressive one. They accepted it at least in the form of a white paper in less than 2 Vt years. They have studied the matter, and the study is now complete. I wonder whether it has proved possible to get the other nations of the world to accept the SI units of measurement of which the minister spoke and whether acceptance of this international unit will have the force of a convention binding on all countries.
I do not begrudge the $7 million which has been spent on this concept, because I believe it is a system which should last for a long time. Children will be able to add in tens-about the only accomplishment I was able to master in the course of my own career in mathematics; you can ask my colleagues, Mr. Speaker, and they will tell you my arithmetic is very bad beyond that point. The metric system does permit a degree of exactness which nothing else will allow.


It is important that the public accept the timetable which the minister has put forward. It is also important that use is not made of devices which the public will not accept or which the public will accept only with reluctance. Unless care is taken, a backlash of resentment will develop against the use of the metric system, especially if the two systems are allowed to be used side by side for a lengthy period of time. I hope a bill will be introduced shortly, expressed in firm language and providing penalties for failure to use the official measurements where established, so that these arrangements will be binding on all Canadians.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE PROGRAM OF GUIDELINE DATES FOR METRIC CONVERSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to speak about the motion of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie), which reads as follows:
That the ... House of Commons approve the government's program of guideline dates for metric conversion;
And that a message be sent to the Senate informing their honours that this House has adopted a resolution approving a program of guideline dates ...
Mr. Speaker, since the tabling in the House of the green paper in 1970, I sincerely believe that this question has progressed very slowly. I still recall the statements of the minister of that time who, when tabling the green paper, stated why the government wanted to introduce the metric system. At that time, he said that it was the British who had maintained for so long the impossible imperial system. They were helped by the United States, a country that used to belong to the British empire and which kept not only the language, but also the archaic measurements of the British government.
Today, Mr. Speaker, more than 110 countries use the system, but I think that the Canadian people might not be ready to accept it. In my opinion, we should urgently prepare Canadians for the introduction of the metric system.
In the United States, the people are doing more or less what we are doing; they are studying and they are wondering how much it will cost. In reading the statements of the minister, I was surprised to learn a few things. He said and I quote:
Let us note that the use of the metric system is legal in Canada since 1873 but that our legislators at that time made the mistake, as their colleagues in the United States ...
. .. and all governments since ...
... not to declare imperial units illegal. Their lack of foresight is now costing us much hardship and money.
At that time, the Metric Commission was created. When he tabled his green paper, the same minister described as follows the advantages of the metric system:
The basic unit of the metric system is the meter which was created in France in 1793 and based on one ten-millionth part (lO7) of a quarter of the earth meridian.
With as well defined a unit which is divided by tens instead of inches, lines and half-lines I feel the metric system is excellent. I see that in the House 90 per cent of all hon. members recognize today the necessity of the metric system. There will always be a small percentage of them, 10 to 15 per cent, who will not want it. Even last
Metric Conversion
week I heard someone say the metric system was impossible. Many things were said to be impossible 20, 30 or 40 years ago which have become possible today. To my mind, there is nothing impossible about adopting the metric system. When 90 per cent of the world population have adopted it, it is high time for the other 10 per cent to follow suit. The minister also indicated there would be difficulties, that some already existed. And he said:
It is often impossible to express precise measures in British units and that is why we often use ordinary fractions.
In the metric system, the smallest unit visible to the naked eye is the millimeter, while in the British system, it is the inch which is twenty-five times greater than the millimeter. The ounce is twenty-eight times greater that the gram.
Minute dimensions in which modern science now deals are impossible to express in our traditional system, but are rather simple in the metric system.
I shall not repeat all those information. They aimed first of all at reassuring the people that the federal Parliament was not embarking on an adventure, but was fulfilling an obligation. The minister said the process was rational and that the population had to go along with it.
Parliament established a commission for metrication. I feel that commission did not put enough emphasis on education. In my view, the commission stressed one main point, judging from what we received from it. I do not know if other members received other reports. I have in hand one six-page report. Considering it cost us $7 million, I feel this is somewhat expensive per page. We should have obtained more information on that commission's work. We read in the report that the commission's main effort was to contact industries. But at the consumer level, it apparently did not make any real effort. I think the first priority should have been consumer education, especially in the school system.
I wonder now how much the commission invested in our schools to help teach the metric system across the country. I am convinced 75 per cent of older people, and by that I do not mean 90- or 95-year olds, but middle-aged people who were educated in the foot-pound system, will be trained by their children. They will teach them how to think in terms of metres. Those who never heard of it will tend, when they try to understand the system, to make comparisons. It takes time, as every French Canadian trying to learn English did experience; at first, he tries to translate the words before speaking. Pretty soon, we will have to think in terms of something else, this time in terms of metres. That will be difficult for those who were trained otherwise. I believe the commission should have emphasized the work to be done in schools. If children are taught to think metric, it will be much easier for industries and even governments to implement that system someday.
The minister was saying this afternoon that he was organizing three pilot projects. Fine! A pilot project is all fine, but it should not last for two or three years, until 1978. While those pilot projects will be carried out in three areas, all the rest of Canada will be waiting. I think that experiment should be carried out throughout Canada, and to begin with children should be taught that system. They would thus be ready for the metric system, and all the rest

Metric Conversion
would follow naturally. That would mean lesser expenses for the government.
The first three pages of the report deal with an academic course to define the metric system. Page four briefly describes the activities of the commission and deals with the approximate cost-
The cost of that broad and ambitious conversion program cannot be estimated with any degree of precision.
I agree with them, for if their progress is going to be so slow, it's also going to be very expensive.
Relationships with the United States are mentioned at the end of the report, which says that metrication is a must for North America. I think that system will be implemented throughout Canada by 1980, and the United States will have to follow suit. However, we should not force that system upon the United States, since Canada always abides by what the United States decide. I am not saying that we should copy from anyone, to see if they will go metric if we don't. Let us get in step with the world because in a couple of years the metric system will be a worldwide phenomenon. We will then have made the step toward progress.
Earlier I heard a representative of the Progressive Conservative Party say, "We will certainly have suggestions to make, we will be inclined to accept the government proposals." Of course I recognize those fears, and Progressive Conservatives are a bit like us when they ask what has the commission done in the past four years. Its work will have to be examined to see if it is serious, if the money was well managed. In those discussions the commission will certainly have to provide more explanations so we can know where we are going. It is all fine to set up guidelines, but we must know in every detail what they can produce.
So we are waiting for all those details so we can know in the next two years what all that might cost at the federal, provincial, municipal, school, industrial, private, public, and parapublic levels. People must know what metric conversion will cost them.
Pilot projects were mentioned. I was somewhat surprised to learn that the minister did not make any federal proposal. It would have been interesting to know his views, and that would have set an example for provincial governments to follow. Unless a few imaginative projects are initiated with respect to the metric system, industries will be increasingly inclined to drag on, and provincial governments will wonder what Ottawa is doing in all that.
I do not know what the views of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce are, but at least today a step was made. We expected something with a little more detail because a lot was expected from that commission. When that commission was set up I thought every year we would be informed, step by step, about what was being done toward metric conversion.
Mr. Speaker, there will be more discussions in committee or in the House. For our part, we are interested in the matter. I heard a while ago the spokesman for the New Democratic Party say that it will be easy in Quebec where there will be much more progess. I admit that it will be probably so. Quebec will go faster in its conversion to the metric system, because in the first place, I think that it

heard about it sooner than other provinces, except perhaps Ontario. It is not surprising. Quebec reacts faster when there is a new development in any field whatever. As for contraception, Quebec has beaten all records. We rank first among provinces for our low birth rate. For high birth rate, we have again beaten the record. We can beat all the records, outmatch all the others and establish the metric system much faster than elsewhere.
I hope that Quebec will show its leadership, since it is now an urgent matter, and establish the metric system to be in harmony with people throughout the world.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE PROGRAM OF GUIDELINE DATES FOR METRIC CONVERSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this very important subject I cannot help but echo the words of the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) and others who have stated we need a proper bill in respect of metric conversion. This is a very important and costly subject in Canada, but to date there has been very little public acceptance. The business community is certainly concerned about metric conversion and to date the glossy brochures full of cartoons are not allaying the fears of businessmen or consumers in this country. It would appear that the $7 million which will be spent by the end of 1975 has not done the selling job for the government and that is why it is important that a proper bill be brought in.
I should like to make some comments in respect of how the metric system is advancing in the United States. They are making some headway, but they are also bringing in some subsidies to help small businesses. I will comment on that in a few minutes. Leading the shift in the United States are large businesses such as General Motors, the nation's largest manufacturer. GM is swinging to a policy of designing all new parts in metrics. This giant firm wants to harmonize production in all GM plants throughout the world. In the U.S. this will affect about 40,000 of GM's suppliers. In addition, Pintos and Mustangs are being equipped with 2.3 litre engines and powered by motors designed entirely in metrics. An estimated 30 per cent to 40 per cent of Ford's production is in foreign markets where metrics are the standard, and a shift in the United States will make parts interchangeable.
In addition, an international panel has agreed on a new standard size for widely used office paper, being 210 by 280 millimetres, which may eventually replace the 8 Vi by 11 inch paper found in most U.S. offices. Many adults will be in for some trying times in computing the new figures but youngsters in many parts of the country are already getting their first taste of the new standards in school. At least 14 states of the United States are in the early stages of preparing class work in metrics and six have enacted laws calling for the metric system to be taught.
In California all elementary school texts must include metrics by 1976, and Maryland has a six-year program of instruction to shift to the new system. Many federal agencies are getting on the metric bandwagon as well, and the U.S. Patent Office is encouraging inventors to include both types of measurements in their patent applications. It would appear that the United States is doing a better


selling job and making better preparations, especially in the educational system, in their country than we are. I will be going into more detail as to the fears in respect of costs of metric conversion on the part of Canadian school boards.
In the United States, however, most experts agree that if the entire nation is to go metric, it must have full federal backing, an idea that has been kicking around since Thomas Jefferson urged the adoption of a decimal system some 150 years ago. I referred to subsidies earlier and I should point out that in the United States they intend to sponsor a bill that would help mechanics pay for the cost of new tools. As an example, an official there argued that a typical machinist who buys his own tools might spend as much as $4,000 for a new set of metric-measured tools. Many small businesses say much the same, that replacing expensive equipment could prove prohibitive. One industrial official in the United States has stated:
There's bound to be a lot of hauling and tugging over the final version of the bill, but if everybody gives a little I think we can finally get the switch to metrication under way.
Some who are in support of the legislation in the United States estimate that the switch could add from $500 million to $700 million in exports per year, and foreign firms could increase their sales to the extent of $300 million to $500 million in the United States.
There have been many meetings across the country, including full-day seminars, to discuss the metric system. I should like to put some of their comments on the record. Mr. J. Kenneth Clark, assistant vice-president of Simp-sons-Sears Limited in Toronto, when speaking to a one-day metric seminar in Toronto sponsored by the Conference Board of Canada stated that no matter to what extent government sponsored commissions, committees and subcommittees indulge in sharing education, in the final analysis it will be the retailer who will bear the burden of educating the reluctant consumer and be the recipient of consumer reaction.
May I call it five o'clock?

He said: Mr. Speaker, although my motion may be considered parochial in nature, I feel its contents, the proposal and its objectives can be relevant on a national basis. It simply asks that the government should appoint, in consultation with the province, a planning and advisory board for western Newfoundland to ensure the steady and orderly progress of the present unprecedented economic development taking place in that part of Canada, and particularly to ensure support for infrastructural, economic, industrial and social and environmental needs, with suggestions for representation on that board.
The west coast of Newfoundland stretches along a coastline of some 500 miles from Port aux Basques in the south to the tip of the northwest coast. I do not intend to trespass on that part of the coast which lies within the responsibility of my colleague the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson), and for the purposes of my exercise will refer only to that greater part of the coast which lies within my own district. Neither is it my intention to cross over into the district of my other colleague the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey), who represents very well the land mass of Labrador almost adjoining; but since there is a very close interrelationship, it is necessary to mention Labrador because the development of the vast energy resources in that part of Canada affects and charges us both with certain responsibilities and emphasizes the need for the special attention and planning which I am requesting through my motion.
In this regard I refer to the provincial government's plans to proceed with the development of the hydro potential of the lower Churchill as follows: the development of the full hydroelectric resources of the Gull Island site, together with a transmission facility for delivery of the power to the island of Newfoundland and an inter-tie with

Western Newfoundland Economic Development
power development on the upper Churchill and the additional island facilities which will be necessary to integrate the existing system. The project, when carried out, will deliver 11 billion kilowatt hours of energy to the island and Labrador, which is equivalent to approximately 18 million barrels of fuel oil annually and would evidently make Newfoundland self-sufficient in her energy needs. Conclusions reached by the consultants indicate that if total financing could be realized of the projected amount of $1.6 billion, then the benefits could be achieved and the output could be absorbed by 1985 to 1988. It is not necessary to point out the importance for Newfoundland, too- because of her isolation-to become self-sufficient in her energy needs. Along with the Come-by-Chance oil refinery and the gas finds off Labrador, this could be realized to ensure not only self-sufficiency but indeed to provide surplus energy to other parts of Canada.
Another important factor in the procurement of energy in our province is to induce mineral exploration and the resulting industrial potential. It is worth while mentioning that I commend the federal government's agreeing to lend the province 50 per cent of the cost of transmission facilities up to $343 million and it now appears that financing will be forthcoming. But coincidental with the resource development is the need to transmit the power to the island via the Strait of Belle Isle in my district at the narrowest point between the two land masses by a cable tunnel 60,000 feet long, 14 feet wide and 17 feet high under the strait to a depth of some 700 feet. As an aside, I am proud to say to the doubters of my private member's bill for the creation of a tunnel to connect the two land masses, which I first introduced in 1968, that the idea was not too far-fetched after all.
I can only hope when the government accepts my motion at the end of this debate that the planning and advisory board which will be created will take as one of its first tasks the ongoing study required to expand the crossing to include the provision of vehicular access, or at least preparation of the design for future additions. But to indicate the magnitude of the project, Mr. Speaker, it is estimated that a labour force of some 600 men would be required in the initial stages, reaching 2,600 men at the peak period.
The figures I mention came out of a study made by consultants which gives in pretty elaborate detail the requirements for the construction of the sophisticated facilities and engineering, but brushes over very lightly the infrastructural support required, such as the need for roads, harbour facilities, third level air service, housing developments, townsites, construction camps and other basic services. This supports my motion in one respect for proper planning to ensure orderly development.
Vast amounts of equipment will have to be transported to the presently isolated location, emphasizing the need for road building, the provision of harbour facilities and the creation of third level airports. It is obvious that there is a need at this very moment to plan that these facilities are provided coincidental with the development of the site. The present road system along the great northern peninsula is entirely inadequate, and while I must give credit again to the minister for his co-operation with the province of Newfoundland in the roads programs which

started last year to support the establishment of the zinc mine in central Newfoundland and the Gros Morne national park, much more needs to be done on an emergency
basis.
Further, shipments of goods and services will have to be made from the ports of Port aux Basques and Corner Brook. As well, lines of transport communications will be required to support the Labrador linerboard mill in Ste-phenville for the movement of the raw resources required between Labrador and the island. Again, Mr. Speaker, even with the financial support over the years to these ports by the federal government, they are congested to the point where expansion is vitally necessary.
So does this, then, not indicate the need for a planning group with elements of MOT and Public Works to become involved right now to ensure orderly progress? And if, as is projected, some 2,600 men will be required, does not this point out the need right now for the Department of Manpower and Immigration to become involved to provide training programs for the jobs required; and since, certainly, there will be a need to bring people in with families from other parts of the province and area and, indeed, the technical skills required from other parts of Canada, is not there a need for orderly housing development for the construction of townsites, to provide water and sewer facilities and to help local school boards to project the needs for expansion of educational facilities?
I ask all members who may participate in this debate, are those people with these specialized skills to move to isolated areas without proper telephone service, without adequate television service and without adequate medical services, which are certainly not adequate in northern Newfoundland? Does this, then, not point out the need for involvement of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) and the Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier) with their provincial counterparts to ensure representation and achieving orderly planning?
What about the effects on the environment and on the quality of life of the proud citizens of those isolated areas who have been oriented primarily to the fast depleting fishing industry? Mr. Speaker, does this not point out the need for involvement by the minister of the environment and fisheries (Mrs. Sauve) with her provincial counterpart? Even in this area of concern I realize that there has just been completed an environmental overview of the lower Churchill power development under the auspices of the provincial government, suggesting measures to minimize principal environmental effects. But these studies tend to get cast aside and it is therefore important that a responsible group be charged with the responsibility to ensure that the recommendations are carried out to the benefit of those Canadians affected.
I might mention, too, the many volumes that make up the trans-Newfoundland corridor transportation study, which does not refer to any inter-tie that is now vitally required in all forms of transportation to the north and again projects the immediate need for further studies to collaborate with the corridor. At this very moment the TransCanada Highway has deteriorated to the point where in order to support this mode of transportation there is the requirement for a strengthening program and expansion of the TransCanada Highway in Newfoundland

to bring it up to a reasonable standard. It is my contention that the TransCanada Highway never, ever, met acceptable standards and if one wanted to look at that highway, or that portion which exists in my district, it would be embarrassing.
But even the industrial progress which can accrue as a result of the energy development cannot be taken in isolation, because along with this development in northern Newfoundland there is ongoing industrial expansion southward along the coastline that I mentioned. I refer to two worth-while projects in the central and southern parts of the Great Northern Peninsula, the establishment of a zinc mine in Daniel's Harbour and the ongoing development of the Gros Morne national park. Already the developers are faced with housing problems, the need for expanded harbour facilities, new road extensions, public services and other needs required to support the movement of people from other adjacent areas to take advantage of the employment offered.
Moving southward again, mention should be made of the ongoing development of the 750 square miles of Gros Morne national park. Under the general development agreement, the federal government is providing 90 per cent of some $15 million for development programs, for community infrastructure and for road construction not only for communities within the park but also for those that are in close proximity and which can benefit economically and socially. This is in addition to some $20 million provided in the current estimates of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, as well as the many millions of dollars that have already been spent in past years. The total sum amounts to $35 million to $40 million. I mention this to reaffirm the need for ongoing planning and orderly progress which would tie in with the development of the northern part of the province.
I am very excited about the industrial progress that is taking place and will continue to take place in the next few years in the most isolated and remote areas of my province. I am optimistic that not only will the benefits accrue to the citizens in that part of Canada but, more important, it will finally allow Newfoundland to compete with other resource-rich provinces and thus enable us to contribute instead of drawing from the wealth of our nation.
However, the development of this vast area of Canada to which I referred cannot be treated in isolation, without consideration being given to the need to solidify the transport base in the southwestern and southern part of our province. I refer to a rectangle formed by the areas of Port aux Basques, Corner Brook, Stephenville and Deer Lake, the more urban areas in western Newfoundland. These areas must be assisted particularly because of their importance as an entry point and point of dispersal to the northern and central parts of Newfoundland.
I repeat that my friend the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion is quite capable of looking after the area he represents in Port aux Basques without my help, but I am sure that he will agree with me that that port plays a vital role in the ongoing development of Newfoundland. My main concern is to remind the government that if we
Western Newfoundland Economic Development are to get full value for the dollars allocated for this purpose, then the transportation base to which I referred must be supported not only with dollars but with common sense planning to ensure the development and progress of the western part of the province.
Taking into consideration the main port of Corner Brook and the allocation of funds in the estimates amounting to $3.5 million, the representation made by the interested parties from that area to expand the present facilities in that natural port must be treated with the utmost urgency. I was most pleased to hear the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion say in committee recently that that expansion proposals would be studied by officials in his department in collaboration with officials in the Department of Transport and the provincial and municipal governments involved.
In addition, we must look at the over-all development of the three areas in the rectangular base before considering each corner of the rectangle. I should like to impress upon members of parliament the importance of this urban centre an the activity which is taking place thereby pointing out that at present a $10 million regional college is under construction. It will be an important urban centre which will need infrastructural support because of the fact that some 500 students will converge there as well as 150 teachers. As a result, there will be the need for a housing development in the area as well as other public services. The main requirement is for the development of an extension for what is known as the Corner Brook-Curling waterfront and the development of the vast potential which exists in western Newfoundland.
Before leaving the subject of the port of Corner Brook, let me refer to the economic heart of the region, the main industry of western Newfoundland, namely, the great Bowater pulp and paper mills which, as well as gypsum and cement plants, have been the mainstay of the economy of the western part of our province and the economic support of the forest resource potential in western Newfoundland. This focuses attention on the need to collaborate with the international enterprise in Newfoundland's forestry policy and in transportation.
I should like to move now to another part of the rectangle and mention another urban centre known as Stephenville, an area which became a prominent and important centre of industry in western Newfoundland. I will not take the time of the House to relate the results of the economic development of that area, but let me say only that now it holds a very important place in the future of Newfoundland because a $200 million linerboard mill is located there, a successful industrial complex. It is part of the urban development of western Newfoundland.
To lend importance to its place in the future development of the province, the mill and the industrial park which form the basis of the economy will receive from the province over $24 million to cover general expenses. It will also obtain the benefits of a subsidiary agreement with the Department of Regional Economic Expansion amounting to $20 million over a four-year period to be used for the construction of access roads and to cover the cost of equipment.
The only remaining part of the rectangle is the town of Deer Lake which serves as the jumping-off point to the


Western Newfoundland Economic Development
Great Northern Peninsula which must also be taken into consideration in the over-all planning of western Newfoundland because of its strategic location as the hub of the north. It must be obvious by now that as a result of the over-all development we must co-ordinate planning, which is the basis of my motion.
I should like to comment on one vital point, namely, the importance of our agricultural potential. I hope that the minister will realize that many parts of western Newfoundland can produce in sufficient quantities to satisfy the agricultural requirements of most of the province. Notwithstanding our mixed industrial potential in the province, any planning that takes place must take fisheries into account. I am sure that members from Newfoundland will agree that any industrial development that exists must take into account the protection of our fishing industry, and I am sure that those who will take part in this debate will support this principle.
Finally, I should like to say that my motion is presented not to criticize but to help. I have described a mixture of almost every type of development in one region of Canada. Newfoundland is as yet comparatively pollution-free, and I feel very strongly that if the government wished to create a model for future planning in Canada, then here is an opportunity which they will never have again. It is in this context that I propose the establishment of a planning and advisory board with representation from departments and agencies at both levels of government to plan and advise for the orderly progress in western Newfoundland which could be used as an example in the future development of our nation. I hope that my motion will be accepted.

speakeroldname: Mr. William Rompkey (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subsubtopic: WESTERN NEWFOUNDLAND-SUGGESTED APPOINTMENT OF ADVISORY AND PLANNING BOARD TO ENSURE ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to take part in the debate on the motion of my colleague, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall). Our areas are contiguous and we have problems in common.
I agree with the essential principle of the motion but I do have some concerns which were reflected in the statement made by the hon. member, and that is that the motion is parochial. That is my only concern and I will comment on it more fully. I have no complaint against the general principle of the motion and I support it. I would not like the motion to be limited to the west coast of the province because that would mean that planning would proceed in that area and might not apply to other parts of the province.
The precedent has been set, I might say, in Goose Bay where the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) over two years ago set up the Goose Bay project group. This project group consists of provincial and federal civil servants, and it was set up to do comprehensive, short-term and long-term planning and implementation of a variety of federal and provincial programs. It is possible that this precedent has been applied elsewhere as well.
It is essential that in the administration of programs in particular areas, people, not only politicians but at the civil service level, get together. As a result of the establishment of the project group, a number of developments

are taking place in the Goose Bay area, an area which at present is very vulnerable economically, but I hope solutions can be found to those problems. There has been co-operative planning between the federal and provincial governments in the whole DREE program in the province. So up to this point the principle has been established.
The hon. member referred to the northern peninsula highway. I was glad to see that last year work started from both ends toward the middle of the highway, which has been in terrible condition until now. The highway is vital for the economic development of the north as well as for the development of the quality of life on the northern peninsula of Newfoundland.
Both of our ridings and the whole province will benefit as a result of the forestry agreement which has been signed with the province. As a result of this, access roads and various other facilities for the lumbering industry and the forest industry in general will be built. I would refer also to the great projects in the field of fisheries: for example, the barge on the Labrador coast last year was largely financed out of federal funds. There will be various marine service centres going in this year, not only in my riding but in that of the hon. member, and I am sure he will agree with me when I say that the program of the federal government for small craft harbours has been of great benefit both for my riding and his. We were able to increase the expenditure to something like $30 million last year in small craft harbours and that program has been of great benefit to many small fishing communities in Newfoundland and in all the Atlantic provinces.
The hon. member referred to the Gros Morne national park, and I congratulate him on having in his area one of the beauty spots of the province. I was glad to hear him give due credit to the federal government for its efforts to improve and to beautify that particular area. There is a smaller version in my riding, Lance aux Meadows, where the first Canadians lived in the year 1000-the Viking site in North America. In the next three years we will be spending a total of $9,000,000 on improvement of that national historic park.
If we are to have co-operation, it must be a two-way street: it must not only be federal, but provincial. I have felt-I do not know how the hon. member feels about this-up until now that we might have had a little more emphasis from the provincial government with regard to the development of northern Newfoundland and Labrador. As far as I can see, most of the funds which have been spent on many of these projects and in many of these areas have been federal funds. I hope we will see a firm commitment in the future on the part of the provincial government to the development of that area of the province.
Co-operation is a two-way street, and if there is going to be an advisory board composed of both levels, there must not only be provincial people on the board but it must be the policy of the provincial government to make a contribution to the further development of those areas. I have not been assured to this time that that firm commitment exists. For example, I notice that a great portion of the provincial budget is put aside for roads, and I cannot see


any of that money going into the Labrador area. Roads are essentially a provincial responsibility. We have spent federal money on roads, but surely the provincial government also has a responsibility along those lines.
If the province is to have a massive road building program this summer with provincial funds, I think it is about time it started spending some money in those areas where it has been noticeably lacking until now. I do not think we can be accused of being political in the allocation of our resources, and I think the hon. member in his comments has agreed with me that the spending of our money has been to try to develop the whole province and not just those sections we might serve. Much more needs to be done. The building of the road up the northern peninsula would certainly open up the area for tourism and encourage people to visit places like the park at Lance aux Meadows.
More needs to be done with regard to the fishery. Much more needs to be done with regard to the lumbering industry. There is a great future for those resources on the northern peninsula of Newfoundland. In central Newfoundland there is already a great deal of economic expansion simply as a result of the base which was there in the beginning, but a great deal still needs to be done. I am referring to water and sewer systems and more roads.
My colleague referred to developments of oil and gas off the Labrador coast, some of the greatest finds in the world. We do not know specifically what the potential is- at least, not from the companies. We are able to guess at it; we certainly know there is a large potential there. We have to be careful when the oil, the gas and, indeed, the hydro are being developed that we make sure, first, that we preserve the environment to protect our fishermen and, second, that we preserve the social structure of the communities. I was very glad to know that recently a team from the provincial government had travelled along that coast and talked with people in various Labrador communities about the possible social implications of oil and gas discoveries and oil and gas development off that coast. The same is true of hydro. The federal government has now funded the native people of Newfoundland in carrying out a study as to their rights with regard to this development. The government is very concerned that in all of this development they will not be shunted aside or neglected in so far as their rights are concerned, and I think we should pay attention to that aspect before we go ahead with this development.
My colleague mentioned that we offered to the province of Newfoundland a loan of $343 million at low interest rates for the building of the transmission line. I agree that that should go ahead and that it is essential. I agree that proper planning should be carried out, but I want to be sure that if and when that hydro development goes ahead, the power is brought across Labrador and used for the whole province and not just a particular section of it. Until now I have not received that firm commitment. The people of Labrador are very concerned that this power will be once more exported and not necessarily used for their own development. We must have a commitment from the developers of the power. It is essential to the whole province but it must also be developed for the people in the
Western Newfoundland Economic Development area where the power source is, and we must have that commitment before the development goes ahead.
I agree in principle with this motion. If we are to implement the principle, then let us do it not only for the west coast but also for other areas in the province. Let us have an advisory board not simply for Goose Bay but also for Labrador. Let us have an advisory board for central Newfoundland and southern Newfoundland and other areas. The principle, though, is well taken. In fact, it is essential. In terms of manpower becoming involved, we have already established a precedent with the community employment strategy. A team from Canada Manpower has been working for some months with officials of the department of social services, I believe, of the province of Newfoundland, and possibly other departments, in trying to structure the community employment strategy. Comprehensive, joint planning between federal and provincial civil servants is going on in the province at this point so far as Canada Manpower is concerned.
The principle is a good one. It should be applied to the west coast, certainly. It should be applied to the northern peninsula, to Labrador, throughout the province, and in other provinces as well. I certainly support in principle the feeling which the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe has expressed, and I wish him well in his commendable and successful efforts in the development of his riding.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the proposal of the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) reminds me, and should remind the House, that he is a Glace Bay boy and a Cape Breton boy and the socialist seems to be coming out in him. He seems to be a socialist in disguise looking for a planning board, so I am happy for him in that regard. I am not sure that the gas finds he and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Rompkey) referred to off Labrador will be as beneficial as he expects for the province, but we can hope, with them, for success in this respect.
I just want to make a few comments about planning, since it is part of the message the hon. member has sought to apply to a particular area of Newfoundland and which his colleague on the other side of the House agreed in principle was needed. When the Atlantic Development Board was set up, it was supposed to come up with a plan for the development of the Atlantic region. This notion seems to have been dropped by the government, for DREE is not really a planning agency, in my opinion, although it should be.
DREE and the Department of Transport are major departments of the federal government which should form the core of a planning board for the Atlantic region. Other federal departments, such as the Department of Public Works and the Department of Fisheries, should attach personnel with at least the status of deputy minister to the proposed planning board. As well, departments of development of all the Atlantic provinces should be included in such a proposed Atlantic regional planning board.


Western Newfoundland Economic Development
Within this planning framework specialized development boards such as the Cape Breton Development Corporation, which is a specialized socio-economic experiment for a depressed area, could serve in Western Newfoundland to fill the role of the sort of planning board proposed by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe.
The proposed Atlantic region planning board would make greater sense if the government gave a commitment to more planning at a national level. Recently Henry Ford III issued a strong warning. North America is undergoing a serious recession and Henry Ford III said that no government today can do without some type of planning mechanism. He was repeating what socialists had long said, that private decision making by corporations often leads to the boom and bust psychology of capitalism, especially corporate capitalism. This leads, on the one hand, to human suffering and severe waste of resources, known as unemployment, and on the other hand, to unstable, inflated prices which are no longer controlled to the same extent as in the past by the private market mechanism. Hence we need to plan how to use our monetary, fiscal and exchange policies to stabilize our economy. There must be planning in some meaningful, national sense.
I believe that economic leadership must be exercised in a new way through a national economic planning board of the sort espoused by the Japanese. This board must be in a position to determine our country's economic and social needs now and for many years to come and provide the public with alternative plans of action. These should not only enable us to avert hardship and disaster, but to guide the economy in a direction consistent with our national values and goals.
I suggest that we are not unfamiliar with the idea of planning. Every individual and business plans for the years ahead. The United States space program is a good example of planning in its most sophisticated and successful form, and illustrates the size of effort which must go into national economic planning. The principles, nevertheless, are simple. First, a set of feasible alternatives was studied, then a realizable goal was set. That goal was the building of a space vehicle to carry a man to the moon and bring him back to earth. To fulfil this mission a long-range program was established. All necessary information had to be gathered in a consistent and useful form; then step by step, the program had to be carried out-

speechtext:
As it is St. Patrick's Day, hon. members' comments may be apt. Allow me to continue. As I said, the space program had to be carried out in the required sequence, the results had to be monitored, and corrections had to be made whenever necessary.
Just as it would have been impossible for a man to go to the moon and back by accident, so it is impossible for us in Canada to achieve our economic objectives by accident. The most striking fact about the way we organize our

economic life is that we leave so much to chance. We give little thought to the direction in which we want to go, and make no consistent effort to balance the needs of different parts of the economy. We do not attempt to ensure that resources are allocated to meet our most urgent national needs. Actually, we know they are not so allocated, as the present state of the economy clearly shows.
We do not try systematically to forecast the needs of the nation in the years ahead. Instead, we use dozens of separate unco-ordinated agencies which make policy in this area and that, without thinking how it all fits together. We have many federal and provincial agencies collecting economic data. In most instances it is insufficiently detailed; frequently, it is obsolete, and often contradictory and incompatible. No single office or agency is responsible for setting appropriate standards and correlating data so that we can pursue coherent national objectives. We make economic policy from quarter to quarter, or year to year, without perspective as to where the economy is going or where we want it to go.
The idea behind planning is simple. On the basis of information, we act. Most of the action in the Canadian economy takes place in the private sector. Democratic planning is not a substitute for a decentralized economy, nor does it replace the millions of private decisions made in the market every day. Instead, democratic planning is needed if we are to reach democratically chosen objectives. It should influence decisions which must be taken in the field of economics. Economic techniques consistent with the attainment of chosen objectives must be used. We already know how these decisions are influenced.
For example, tax incentive or disincentive measures and traditional monetary and fiscal policies directly influence individual actions. Selective credit controls, measures governing basic capital flows, and other measures involving limits to the use of air, water and land, and mandatory resource allocation affect individual actions directly. All such measures have been used at one time or another by the federal government in a haphazard fashion, except in World War II, with no consideration of their over-all effect. The purpose of planning is to take over-all effect into account.
It should be clear that the proposed planning office would not set specific goals for General Motors of Canada, General Electric, or any other individual firm. The office would determine the number of cars, generators, and so on, and the amount of frozen food we might need, say, in five years, and try to induce relevant industries to act accordingly. In such a way the plan would supplement and reinforce the market and have it serve the public interest. This is not happening now.

speechtext:
Other members will want to speak on this motion because the suggestion contained in it could be applied in many other regions of Canada, especially rural areas. Many small towns and villages simply do not have the resources to establish individually the kind of advisory board I think the hon. member has in mind. So there is no doubt in my mind that the two senior levels of government must be prepared to play a greater and more direct role in ensuring good and orderly development of the more depressed regions of Canada.
I know from researching this proposal that western Newfoundland, containing 18 per cent of the population of the province, faces special circumstances. Some sections of the economic base need considerable improvement. The unemployment levels of the area have been higher than those of the province as a whole, and in the manufacturing sector growth has been only marginal.
Successive federal and provincial governments have attempted in various ways to improve this situation, but not until the Department of Regional Economic Expansion was established in 1969 did the federal government begin a concerted, fully organized effort to attack regional disparity. Since then there has been a proliferation of joint federal provincial undertakings involving not only DREE but other federal authorities such as Manpower, CMHC and Fisheries.
During this period DREE introduced various programs and signed a number of important agreements which have been of economic benefit to western Newfoundland. For the record, I would like to refer to some of them. Under the special areas agreement, as amended, three regions in western Newfoundland were designated: Corner Brook, Hawkes Bay-Port au Choix and Stephenville. The estimated cost of the agreement was $39.9 million. Of this amount DREE will provide $19 million in contributions and $20.9 million in loan funds. These projects included the construction of schools, highways, water and sewer systems.
