speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to continue my remarks in regard to metric conversion, at five o'clock I was quoting some comments reportedly made by Mr. J. Kenneth Clark, who is the assistant to the vice-president of Simpsons-Sears of Toronto. The article continues:
He noted that the retailing industry is progressively becoming more self-serve, "forcing the customer to become more self-reliant," and thereby reducing the role of the sales person.
The cost of conversion to metric units for pre-packaged, non-food products after August 31, 1975, will be considerable, Mr. Clark said, but the change will probably not register with most consumers.
Metric Conversion
"If it is noticed at all it will probably be thought of as information placed there for the convenience of new Canadians who have recently come to Canada from Europe."
But when hard conversion (changing containers to even metric sizes) takes place, Mr. Clark speculated that "there may be a boom in the sale of conversion texts, slide rules and rulers."
But for retailers, the problem with hard conversion will be a proliferation of sizes. "I understand that the men's dress shirt industry in the United Kingdom will now grade collar sizes in one centimetre intervals in place of the historical one-half inch.
"This will increase the number of collar sizes offered from eight to 11. This increase may cause little concern to the merchants in Britain because they do not offer a choice of sleeve lengths. If we were to follow suit, our stockkeeping units would increase from 24 to 33 per colour or pattern.
"However, it is possible that by grading in two centimetre intervals from 35 to 45 centimetres we could reduce the number of collar sizes offered from eight to six and our stockkeeping units from 24 to 18 and still provide an acceptable fit for our customers."
One of the more serious problems faced by retailers will be in maintaining inventory of parts manufactured using both metric and avoirdupois units.
"When the appliance industry converts to metric, the retailer or his supplier will have to maintain a long term inventory of parts manufactured to both standards. The same is true of plumbing fixtures and
systems".
Those are a few of the comments made by Mr. Clark in regard to the problems facing business in Canada and why it is important that a proper bill be brought in to deal with the metric conversion program.
I should like to refer to some further comments made to the Conference Board in Canada recently. It was claimed that the federal government's information program to educate consumers on the metric system is inadequate. Elizabeth Bond, chairman of a sector committee of the Metric Commission in Canada, told a one-day seminar on the metric system in Toronto that there was little hope for improvement in the near future. She noted that the greatest obstacle to conversion to a metric system lies in the groundless fears of consumers. Her committee has attempted to come to grips with the over-riding need for consumer education by creating a public information subcommittee. However, the committee remains unconvinced that it has had any major impact upon the commission's program or lack thereof. Sadly, this means that much of the information burden must remain with the private sector.
This is why we are questioning this $7 million expenditure. The government seems to have done a very poor selling job; it has not got the message across to the Canadian people or manufacturers.
In addition, fears expressed by small businessmen have been pointed out by Mr. John Bulloch, the federation president for Canada's 650,000 small business proprietors. He claims that these businessmen cannot mind their stores and pay for Canada's conversion to the metric system at the same time, and the Canadian Federation of Independent Business has so advised Ottawa. Mr. Bulloch, the federation president, has called for financial and technical aid to help small and medium sized business absorb the impact of conversion. As I pointed out earlier today, Mr. Speaker, the United States is bringing in a system of subsidies to help, for example, mechanics, and this is something that will have to be done in Canada.
28996-S9'/2

Metric Conversion
Mr. Bulloch told the Conference Board in Canada that a milligram of prevention is worth a kilogram of cure. He was referring to the federal policy of allowing the costs of conversion to fall where they may. His remarks were made in a speech to the board's Toronto conference on the impact of metric conversion on North America. Mr. Bulloch went on to say:
We recommend a program of grants and low-interest loans to assist in the financing of metric conversion.
Mention was made earlier today that we should have a system of low cost loans, and I hope that the minister will give this serious consideration. Mr. Bulloch continued:
Large companies have technical, financial and managerial resources for planning their own metric changeover and dealing with it over the long haul. Small businesses do not. It is the responsibility of government to ensure that small businessmen, including self-employed craftsmen, are properly informed and their interests adequately understood and represented.
Mr. Bulloch criticized the use of the federal Metric Commission to "implement a program for the entire nation before the policy decisions have been fully approved at the parliamentary level."
Small business is concerned that decisions are being made by administrators before legislators have done their homework.
"The work of the commission should receive parliamentary examination and approval immediately. It is difficult to expect provincial governments and business to be in metric changeover planning so long as there has been no bill or joint resolution before parliament.
Also Mr. Speaker, Mr. J. H. Kluge, President of Ascolec-tric Ltd. of Brantford told a seminar on the metric conversion program:
Some companies or industries will be hard hit by foreign imports once the Canadian market is open to products now being sold in the metric world, but which could not sell here because our market was too small for them to make special designs in imperial dimensions.
He further stated:
Government and industry will have to co-operate to a degree as never before to avoid a loss of employment in the secondary manufacturing industry.
Mr. Kluge said that timing was critical and:
We must avoid opening the market to foreign imports before the domestic manufacturers are ready to compete on even terms.
Conversely, there are many opportunities that will be presented to Canadian businesses. Mr. Kluge stated:
If a company is not prepared for this change it may become a traumatic and costly experience later on.
The article continues:
He noted that the impact of metric conversion on Canada's foreign trade cannot be generalized. "About $1.5 billion or 8 per cent by value of our 1973 export may be affected sharply. This amount of export must and will increase as new opportunities are realized."
He further stated:
Industrial management has been urged to invite union participation in planning for conversion to the metric system to avoid disputes arising from fear of change.
The article then continues as follows:
A. S. Tirrell, Canadian Labour Congress representative to the Metric Commission, told the Conference Board in Canada that relatively few union members would be directly affected by the conversion at their places of work but "there will be substantial segments of the work force where the effects will be impressive and critical.
"It is within such segments that Canada can ill afford any serious dislocation of the work force, with its resultant unrest and turmoil."

He said labour considers metric conversion inevitable and desirable but the willingness of workers, through understanding and fair dealing, to accept the conversion is vital.
"All unions will take actions to ensure that their members are not adversely affected, regardless of the degree to which their jobs are measurement sensitive. They will attempt to protect their members against loss of income, employment security, promotional opportunity, job mobility, and against the burden of any costs additional to those which may be already borne by them.
"Managements would be wise to take the unions into their confidence and afford them participation in the planning process."
I have received representations from many businessmen in my riding, and I should just like to read part of the
comments of one of them. He said:
We fabricate and supply reinforcing steel for reinforced concrete construction. Our products are used entirely within two prairie provinces and we do not engage in overseas trade. Changing to the metric system will greatly increase our costs due to a complete change of our measuring system. We believe that the change to the metric system will greatly increase costs in Canada and will not accomplish anything except for a few firms engaged in overseas trade. These firms should gear up for the dual system of metric and English standards and bear the cost in order to engage in their particular market.
This gentleman studied the situation and could see no benefits for his particular firm. He suggested that all this was going to do was add to the cost of manufacturing his product, and of course this will be passed on to the consumer, contributing to higher inflation.
Even as late as last week there were comments in the news media in respect of the metric conversion program. I should just like to read a few comments made by Mr. Gerald Hodge, the Director of the School of Urban and Regional Planning at Queen's University. He states:
In the sixties you were given to understand that when you passed 30 you were over the hill. In this metrication decade, the cataclysmic year has reached right down to the pre-adolescents.
One Montreal educator thinks that anyone beyond Grade 5 (10 years old) will never fully adjust to the metric system.
You're probably not much awed by this prospect. This may mean that the Canadian Metric Commission has already got you to think metric. Or it may indicate a certain resignation to the thrust of events; the Metric Commission seems to have convinced a lot of businessmen, newspapers, labour unions, etc., to say "it's inevitable".
Or it could be simple, old apathy and, in that case, maybe there is still some hope that this momentous step won't be taken in such a sheeplike way by Canadians.
Have you ever wondered, as I have, why this country is involved in such a specious exercise? Who benefits from metrication? Who pays? Are the advantages as substantial as the claims for the metric system
suggest?
There are three general areas in which we are being led to expect extensive payoffs by converting Canada to the metric system of measurement. These are (1) manufactured goods sold in world export markets, (2) the learning capabilities of people, and (3) simplicity and convenience in packaging, purchasing and quality-control. Let's examine each of these areas and test the validity of the claims.
(1) World export markets will be thrown wide open to our manufacturers if we become a metric country. "It has been estimated," the reports always seem to say, "that Canada loses between $100 million and $200 million in foreign trade a year" because it has not yet converted. The Metric Commission confidently reports that exports should increase up to 10 per cent.
This is mere pie-in-the-sky. Consider two aspects of this matter.
First, world markets are not just sitting there waiting for us to exploit them by making sure our screws fit and our sizes are the same. A lot of pretty efficient firms in other countries know these sources of wealth, too.

Second, world trade is a two-way business. Once the Canadian scene is metricated it will be an easy matter for foreign firms producing for the metric world to expand production and export to us. That old imperial system of feet, inches, gallons and quarts, it seems, acts somewhat as a "tariff barrier" in favour of our firms.
Look around you at all the products made in metricated countries such as Japan, Italy, Sweden and Czechoslovakia. They may be made to metric scale such as your toaster, your Toyota, or your transistor and you never really gave it a thought, or had to. When was the last time you had a problem getting a French bicycle, an Italian auto, or a Japanese hairdryer fixed because it was a metricated unit?
You may have had troubles for lots of other reasons, but not likely for the measurement scale it was designed in. And much the same applies to the Spaniard driving a British car or the Swede using a U.S. computer.
It was mentioned earlier in the debate today that the school boards are concerned about metric conversion. I have some correspondence here from the Manitoba Association of School Trustees. They state in part:
Last spring, MAST took a very quick look at the cost implications of conversion to the metric system. That study indicated that costs of conversion for the academic stream would be about $4 per pupil and about $50 per pupil in the vocational area.
Who is to pay these increased costs? Will they be paid by increases in municipal taxes or will the provinces come up with the money? This is a very costly item and that is why a proper bill should be brought in on metric conversion so it is properly debated in the House and in committee rather than being put through as a resolution. The association went on to say:
Please keep in mind that the above figures were developed from a very superficial and quick study-your cost determinations might be substantially different.
Metric conversion is a federal policy and will be a fact by 1980. Because it is a federal policy our position has been that the implementation of such federal policy should be at the cost of the federal government.
Here is another statement made by Mr. Donald Eyles, President of Metricanada Consultants, a company formed to advise private and government organizations on metric conversion. Mr. Eyles stated:
Metric conversion in Canada is rapidly becoming a mess. Contrary to the unctuous platitudes coming out of Ottawa the Canadian metric conversion program is characterized by political expediency, indecisiveness and, above all, lack of leadership.
Understanding our predicament requires some background information. The basic question-'Why are we going metric anyway?'-has a simple (and perhaps unpalatable) answer:
The critical factor in the matter of North American adoption of metric measurement has been the emergence, since World War II, of the U.S. international corporations that now largely dominate U.S. foreign and domestic policy.
These multinationals have, between them, about 3,000 overseas manufacturing plants with an annual production valued at $225 billion-half the parent companies' total production. These 'global' companies want standardization in their operations, particularly in design, which leads to interchangeability of parts.
The domestic effect on the U.S. of the independent adoption of metrics by the multinationals is already immense. Two years ago a few major companies, including GM, recognizing the increasing impact of their direct suppliers alone (the top few multinationals are believed to have between 200,000 and 250,000 suppliers) required their metric programs to be co-ordinated. They formed the American National Metric Council to provide the necessary co-ordination and in two years the council has attracted well over 1,000 members whose names read like a Who's Who of American industry.
Metric Conversion
Various U.S. (and Canadian) government agencies are members, as well as a few Canadian private companies (Metricanada included).
A U.S. bill that would have set up a federal co-ordinating body failed to pass last May for procedural reasons. Indications are that a new bill will be presented to the Congress in a short while with good chances of passage.
However, our own federal government considers it politically expedient to await the U.S. legislation so that all blame for what undoubtedly will antagonize a few voters can 'officially' be directed at Washington.
Canada still lacks any private company or industry group, free of U.S. control, that could assume the initiative for metric conversion taken years ago by the U.S. multinationals.
As just one example, take the construction industry, with its many components. There are owners, developers, subcontractors, tradesmen from sheet-metal workers to bricklayers, various professional bodies, component manufacturers and government regulatory bodies.
Some people in construction have been pressing for a deadline in 1977 after which all construction components would be standardized in metric terms: agreed dimensions for bricks, concrete blocks, steel joists, door frames, plywood sheets-and on and on.
The problem is that buildings that'll go up in 1977 are being designed right now. The designers need to know what component sizes to use. The component manufacturers don't want to change their present specifications until they know whether there's a demand for new ones.
The complexity of the industry isn't really the problem; it's the lack of leadership. In this particular industry the federal government could exercise dominant leadership through its Department of Public Works.
When the federal government published a White Paper on Metric Conversion in January, 1970, it obviously did not foresee the political hot potato it would later become. The guidelines for conversion established at that time were essentially that conversion should be voluntary but co-ordinated and that there would be no subsidies for any costs incurred.
So one can see the concern there is in the country. Many businesses will have serious problems in dealing with metric conversion. Mr. Eyles closes by saying:
I do know, from unsolicited testimony, that many people involved with metric conversion committees, some at Metric Commission level, are beginning to feel that their time and expense is wasted. Meaningful decisions are not being made. The Weary Willies and Tired Tims exploit the timidity and indecisiveness fostered by a leadership vacuum-leadership we properly expect from our national government.
I cannot help but emphasize that we need a separate and individual bill rather than this resolution in dealing with metric conversion. This matter is far from being made clear to the public and the business community all over Canada, and should be still further considered by a standing committee.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE PROGRAM OF GUIDELINE DATES FOR METRIC CONVERSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a sound and accurate system of measurement has been fundamental for civilization from earliest times. One way this is shown is by the many references in both the Old and New Testaments to weights, measures and balances. The Old Testament in Leviticus commands that "ye shall do not unrighteousness in weight or in measure". The prophet, Micah, complains of "the scant measure that is abominable".
The motion before the House involves a decision that is one of the most significant that members of parliament can be called on to make, although this may not seem to be so at first glance. Our system of weights and measures is not only important to our ability to exchange goods and services within this country and with the world, it is also part of the essential fabric of our daily existence in an organized society.

Metric Conversion
When it decides on this resolution the House will be taking a formal position for the first time on the idea that this country should change from its traditional inch-pound system of measurement to the metric system. However, the House is being asked by the government to say not simply whether a change to the metric system is desirable in principle, but instead that it approves the government program of guideline dates for metric conversion.
One would have thought therefore that these dates would be spelled out fully in the resolution. Curiously enough, the government has not done this. I wonder how the government can expect the House to make a decision with such far-reaching implications for every Canadian without even putting before it formally the basic information required to give the resolution any meaning.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) may give such information in his speech in support of the resolution, but this is not the same as stating it formally in the resolution itself. The failure to do this gives no opportunity to members of parliament to consider and do research on the suitability of the guideline dates prior to the beginning of the debate on the resolution. It means that this consideration can be given only during the debate itself which, unless it is lengthy or is adjourned, or unless the resolution is referred to a committee, does not provide an adequate opportunity, in my view, to examine basic and fundamental aspects of the matter.
One can also ask why the government is asking the House to deal with this important matter by resolution. A resolution does not have the legal force of an act of parliament. It is not binding on anyone in the sense that not following it would bring any criminal or civil sanction.
Using a resolution in a matter such as this has at least one major flaw from the point of view of parliamentary consideration of the question at issue. The flaw is that when the House considers a resolution, our rules do not provide any automatic provision for committee study of the resolution or its subject matter, as is the case with most bills. This means that we have no opportunity to question the minister or his officials directly and in detail on the practical effect of metric conversion on our daily lives and our commercial activity, both domestic and foreign, nor can we question them on the costs of this conversion and how they will be assumed.
We are unable to hear the views on these matters of witnesses from business, labour and consumer groups, as well as concerned citizens who are not formally members of any of these kinds of organizations. We cannot question the minister, officials, and people outside the government on whether the dates proposed for metric conversion, whatever they may be, are in fact the best for any particular industry sector in the light of the circumstances most relevant to that sector.
As I have said, the resolution does not in fact set out any guideline dates at all. However, a body called the Metric Commission has developed its own ideas as to what they should be. According to a document published by the

Metric Commission entitled "Canada Prepares for Metric Conversion":
In September of 1973 the Canadian Metric Commission outlined a list of target dates for the project. They proposed that the four phases-investigation, planning, scheduling and implementation-be completed by the end of 1980 when the normal day to day transactions in the economy would be entirely in metric units.
The publication goes on to say:
The investigation phase is now under way and should reach its peak in 1974. The planning and scheduling phases will extend through 1974 and 1975 with a view to being substantially completed in 1976. According to the proposed targets, implementation should start in 1975 and reach its peak in 1977-1978, although some industries would no doubt continue operating with the imperial units for a longer period.
The commission in effect calls for one single implementation date of 1980 for the entire economy, with no indication as to why it considered that date suitable for all sectors in it. The minister in his speech today has endorsed that date and the others developed by the Metric Commission. Even in the absence of an opportunity for committee study of the resolution, I think the House can insist that the government prove its case that the guideline dates that it is proposing are the best ones for the country or, for that matter, any guideline dates are appropriate and needed.
In January of 1970 the government tabled in the House a white paper on metric conversion in Canada. In that white paper the government took the position that:
The eventual adoption and Canadian usage of a single coherent measurement system based on metric units should be acknowledged as inevitable and in the national interest.
However, I should say that nowhere in the white paper did the government say it would be proposing a system of guideline dates. Instead it pointed out with regard to the implementation of metric conversion "there will be wide variation from sector to sector" and that "wide flexibility in timing would appear to be necessary". In other words, the Metric Commission beginning in 1963 has developed a set of guideline dates, including one for implementation, which would be the same for the entire economy. However, the government's original white paper called for a high degree of flexibility on this with, what I would take to be, dates varying by sector rather than one final date for all sectors, a date now only a few years away.
According to the white paper the government appeared to be taking this position because of the differing circumstances and the resulting cost considerations in many sectors of the Canadian industry. The white paper stressed that this was particularly important because "change would likely be closely related to progress in the United States toward conversion, reflecting the complex interlocking of industrial technology in North America." The white paper went on to say:
At present, it is the United States market which absorbs a major and increasing share of Canada's exports of manufactured goods. Some major sectors of Canadian industry are closely involved corporately and in respect of technology with the United States. This linking of industry in the two countries extends to markets both in North America and beyond. In these cases, it may prove wise to allow the timing and process of conversion to be closely related to the development of United States practice.
Yet the government has provided little information as to whether the guidelines it is proposing are in fact consistent with the pace of metric conversion in the United States. It is my understanding that, in point of fact, we are

ahead of the United States. The United States Congress last year refused to pass a law committing that country to metric conversion by certain specific and fairly early dates.
While we are concerned about the degree to which our best customer continues to be the United States, this is one of the facts of our current existence. Any effort to build up a new trading link with Europe and other parts of the world to lessen our dependence on the United States market, although welcome, will take some time to develop. One can also wonder to what extent this option will be able to replace in fact our links with the United States market which is still the largest and most wealthy one in the world today.
One can also question the appropriateness of a government body, the Metric Commission, developing as early as in 1963 a set of target dates to implement metric conversion, and going on to work with business and industry to reach these goals without any parliamentary approval. One can question the appropriateness of the government coming along to ask for such approval only when the commission itself is well along in the final implementation phase.
In fact the commission appears to have been given by the government a role far beyond what the government said in its policy white paper the commission would have. This document said only that there would be "a full-time preparatory commission ... appointed to advise upon and co-ordinate overall planning of the conversion process".
One can ask how the commission came to have the task of actually overseeing the implementation of the conversion process, rather than being limited to co-ordinating its planning.
I have asked whether a resolution is the best parliamentary means to examine adequately the suitability of the government's program of guideline dates. We are dealing with a very serious issue. The suitability of these dates has a lot to do with the ability of our economy effectively to carry on both domestic and foreign business, its ability to meet import competition and, above all, it has a lot to do with what the actual costs may be for business and industry, and therefore ultimately for the public, of converting to the metric system.
If this is a matter of serious concern for any sector of Canadian industry, in my view it is crucial for a sector such as the auto industry which is highly integrated with its counterpart in the United States. The Canadian auto industry does not simply export much of its final production to the United States. Canadian manufactured parts are exported to the United States to be incorporated, along with American manufactured parts, in cars assembled in that country. These cars are then sold in both Canada and the United States. American manufactured parts are imported into Canada to be incorporated, along with Canadian manufactured parts, in cars assembled here which are sold in both the United States and Canada.
How can an implementation date of 1980 be practical for the Canadian auto industry unless this is the firm date for the American auto industry as well? What assurance can the minister and the government give us that there will be
Metric Conversion
identical and parallel guideline dates for both of these industries?
There is at present concern about the future of the Canadian auto industry and employment in it because of the decline of the American economy. We have to be certain, therefore, that the government's pace of moving to the metric system in Canada will not be such as to give the American parent companies an excuse not to carry out further investment in new plants and equipment in Canada, or to transfer production to the United States to serve the needs of that market.
I have made reference to the cost of metric conversion. The white paper and the Metric Commission's own publications keep saying that benefits will outweigh costs, although they never give us any detailed cost benefit analysis to back this up, Mr. Speaker. I am, however, inclined to think that over a period of time the benefits of metric conversion, properly handled, will in fact outweigh the costs, but this will not necessarily be the case in the short or medium term for every industry or every Canadian. Until today the government has not shown any interest in special programs to help those Canadian businesses which will be forced to bear a greater share of the burden of moving to metric conversion than others in the economy. The program announced today does nothing about dealing with the additional cost to workers who have to buy their own tools.
The government has until today always taken the position that since all Canadians will ultimately benefit, the costs should lie where they fall. However, this overlooks the fact, as I have said, that metric conversion will likely carry a greater burden for some Canadians than for others, and some are better able to deal with these cost burdens than others.
It is likely that large businesses with a high degree of economic power will be better able to absorb the costs, or what is more likely, to pass them on to the public in the form of higher prices. This is something which cannot be done by the small businessman or the independent skilled tradesmen or the worker. It will be harder for many small businesses than for larger ones to absorb additional costs of metric conversion arising out of maintaining dual inventories of goods or replacement parts, as well as the cost of converting or replacing machinery and weighing devices. Again, as I have said, the government's program announced today, while helpful, contains a serious omission. It will not be available to help workers.
Many workers who are not self employed have to provide their own tools. For example, it can cost an auto mechanic up to $2,000 for a full set of mechanic's tools. The $150 income tax deduction for employment expenses is obviously no help to a worker in dealing with these kinds of unusual costs.
There is already a precedent for the government taking special measures in the interests of an entire economy when it causes the restructuring of an industry. These special measures are used to help those businesses and workers on whom it is found the burden of the cost of this restructuring falls in greater measure than on the rest of the population. One example of this is what the govern-

Metric Conversion
ment did to create special programs to help both firms and workers in the auto industry to adjust to the extra cost and dislocation caused by the change in that industry created by the auto pact.
I believe that in the course of this debate the government should give a commitment that it will help not only Canadian small businessmen but also Canadian workers to bear any additional special burden caused by conversion to the metric system. Carrying out this commitment could require programs of special grants, or low interest loans, or special tax exemptions not only for business and also for workers who have high one-time costs for replacing tools and equipment which they must supply out of their own pockets.
It has not been proven that metric conversion will benefit all Canadians equally, certainly not in the short and medium term. This is unlikely to be the case for a host of small businesses serving the domestic market, especially in the retail and service field. This is not so for the skilled tradesmen and repairmen who also serve the local market. Therefore the government must make the kind of commitment to which I have referred for additional measures of assistance in these kinds of cases, not only for business but also for workers.
There is another area of concern which the government appears to have overlooked. I refer to the possibility that some unscrupulous elements in the business world will use the changeover to the metric system to increase profits unjustly at the expense of consumers. They would in effect use the opportunity to increase their profit margins by maintaining the same price even when they shift to supplying their product in a metric size, which in fact is somewhat smaller than the size previously used. For example, the consumer might have the general idea that the metric measure for volume closest to the quart is the litre, and that the metric measure closest to a three pound package in weight is the kilogram. However, the litre is equal to only some 88 per cent of the volume of a quart. A kilogram is equal to only 2.205 pounds. Obviously if an unscrupulous businessman charges the same for a litre of his product as he does for a quart, this will mean a substantial price increase for the consumer and a substantial increase in profits for the businessman.
The government has not said that it will have any special program to prevent the consumer from being ripped off in the way I have outlined. It has said nothing about creating any mechanism to prevent this rip off from occurring, to impose sanctions on anyone attempting to take advantage of the consumer in this way, and to get redress for the consumer where, in spite of the sanctions, this is found to have occurred.
A businessman might say that metric conversion means added costs which he had to recover through increased prices, but these increased costs would not go on forever. They would be recovered over a certain limited number of sales in the future. The government has proposed no mechanism, as I have said, whereby these claims could be checked out and the businessman subjected to appropriate sanctions unless he was found to have passed on only the actual true additional cost of conversion.
Our laws on misleading advertising, and packaging and labelling have not been set up to deal with the precise

kind of situation I have outlined today. The unscrupulous businessman, would probably not actually be advertising that he is providing the same quantity for the same price as before metric conversion. He will be improving his profit margins by taking advantage of the unfamiliarity of the consumer with the new system in comparison with the existing inch-pound system, as well as of the difficulty the average consumer would have in making the calculations necessary to find out the facts.
The government's request that the House approve guidelines for metric conversion is another argument for the speedy presentation by the government and the implementation of the anti profiteering bill. However, such a bill, whether it is called "anti profiteering'.' or "price justification", would be only a partial answer to the problem. It would likely be designed to apply primarily to broad categories of goods and services rather than to a large number of individual transactions in many areas of the economy.
The present Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) told both the Financial Post and the Financial Times last fall that he considers such a bill to be "window dressing" and that he hopes he will never have to use it. In addition, the effect of such a bill in preventing the consumer from being taken advantage of by unscrupulous businessmen during metric conversion is hypothetical since such a bill has not yet been presented to the House by the government, and there is no firm indication when it will do so. In any event, I think there is need for a special government measure in addition to an anti profiteering bill to deal with the special problem metric conversion can cause to consumers.
There is also a great need for a better information program to educate consumers about the metric system and metric conversion. According to the Globe and Mail on Wednesday, December 18, Elizabeth Bond, who, I think, is a consumer representative and chair person of a Metric Commission sector committee on consumer aspects of conversion, told a conference board seminar that the federal government's information program to educate consumers in the metric system was inadequate. The article said that her committee has attempted to come to grips with the overriding need for consumer education by creating a public information subcommittee. However, the committee, according to the article, remains unconvinced, and I quote:
... that we have had any major impact on the commission's program or lack thereof.
I think the points I have outlined demonstrate why more than what may turn out to be a relatively brief general debate in this House is required in order for members of parliament to make a wise decision as to whether they approve the government's program for metric conversion. Detailed answers to the kinds of questions I have raised today in a positive and constructive sense are required. But these can come only from the kind of study of the resolution that can best be provided by a parliamentary committee. I hope it will be possible to refer the resolution to a committee for this purpose.


The government, before a final decision is taken on this resolution, should also give commitments that it will provide help for both small businessmen and workers on whom the cost burden of conversion will fall more heavily than on others in the economy. It must also give consumers a commitment that it will firmly and actively protect them against the kind of rip-off I have described that is possible during the course of metric conversion.
I want to recognize the useful work of the Metric Commission and, in particular, the work of the volunteer members from many industry and community groups on its sector committees. But many small businessmen and workers, as well as many individual Canadians, do not belong to any of the organizations represented on the sector committees. It is not the Metric Commission and those committees which will be held accountable by the Canadian public for the effects and costs on them of metric conversion. Instead, the public will look to its elected members of parliament.
Therefore the ultimate responsibility to the people of Canada as a whole for this kind of decision is that of the members of parliament. Therefore members have a responsibility to have the government carry out metric conversion in ways that effectively deal with the problems I have outlined. In doing so the government will be carrying out the general commitment expected of it on this by Canadians, a commitment which, if I may conclude as I began, can be expressed in the words of the Old Testament, in Deuteronomy, as that of providing "a perfect and just weight-a perfect and just measure" or, in the words of the New Testament, in Luke, as "good measure pressed down and running over."
Ensuring that the government carries out this commitment should be the objective of all in this House as they consider and decide on this important resolution on metric conversion.

Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to speak after the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray). Let me say amen to many of the things he said. I listened with interest to what many participating in this debate said, and will not repeat their ideas. Let me make this point, however. I am not alone in being concerned about metric conversion. A lady who came to my office this past week end wanted to know about metric conversion, and wanted to submit a petition to the minister which would express the concern of the group she represents. I told her that unless the petition was presented by Sunday it would be too late, as this measure would be before the House early this week. Metric conversion in Canada would be as certain as death and taxes. I think we know how certain death and taxes are.
After a certain date, temperatures will be announced on the radio and television in degrees Celsius. Many people will not know how to convert degrees Celsius into degrees Fahrenheit, at least not for a while. Therefore I think that the temperature should be announced in degrees Celsius and Fahrenheit until people get used to the metric scale. I talked with my honoured and knowledgeable colleague in the medical profession and said, "I know my normal temperature in degrees Fahrenheit is 98.3; what is it in degrees

When I was a student many years ago arithmetic was probably my worst subject. I see my leader smiling at me. Perhaps he thinks I was bad in many more subjects. Be that as it may, I am told that sums in the metric system will be much easier to do, so there is some consolation for those who are poor at arithmetic. I am told that anybody under the age of ten will not have trouble with the metric system. My six-year-old grandson is already learning in the metric system and having more fun than I ever had.
Small businessmen in Canada worry about how much conversion will cost in dollars and cents. The whole question boils down to this: are they to make a little money from their operation, or are they to pour money into a conversion process which they may not be able to recoup? The previous speaker and others mentioned mechanics tools. Mechanics will be allowed up to $150 for conversion. That is not enough. I hope the minister will consider introducing a training program and pay mechanics for time they must take off work in order to learn the new system.
As other speakers have mentioned, it will cost merchants a great deal to convert scales to metric measurement. Recently I had lunch with a man who owns a fair-sized I.G.A. store in Ottawa. He said he had bought a pair of scales for $9,000. He said that it would cost at least $4,000 to convert them. I thought he would still be ahead by $5,000, but he said no, he would have to scrap those scales and buy a new set. I am told that it will cost 28,000 odd retailers around $50 million to convert, and that is a conservative estimate. We know that much of the conversion cost will be tax deductible. Nevertheless, many small corner store businessmen are not making enough to pay taxes, let alone enough to pay for conversion. Perhaps the minister would consider giving such people a grant, to enable them to convert when the time comes.
We are told that the United States is embarked on a conversion program but that it is proceeding more slowly than we are. In my view both countries should convert at the same pace. It is well known that over 69 per cent of our trade is with the United States. Therefore we should not move more quickly than that country in converting to the metric system, or we may be the losers. An hon. member mentioned that conversion bills have come before Congress for the past three years, but none has passed so far. Certainly conversion has been discussed in that country, and they know it is coming.
I am a real estate broker and metric conversion will open a can of worms for my profession. It will be extremely difficult to convert measurements on present land deeds to the metric system. I admit that the idea of inches, feet, chains and rods may be complicated. However, if we start now to convert all the deeds in Canada which are on the old basis, they probably will not all be converted for 500 years. Not too many of us will be around then. However, this is something which must be seriously considered.

I believe that 94 per cent of the population has now converted to the metric system. That figure was staggering to me. As I understand it, one half of the world trade in dollars is still on the English unit system. Granted, a tremendous amount of that trade is with the United States.
This brings me to another point. Previous speakers have mentioned the cost of conversion and the fact that a cost benefit for Canada has not been done. We do know that this will cost the Canadian taxpayer a great sum.
I understand the United States National Bureau of Standards did a cost benefit analysis. The net cost will be $45 million. That is a lot of money. There has been criticism of that figure. Even if they cut $10 million off the figure, it would still be a lot of money.
The case has not been proved in Canada as to the exact dollar benefits we will get. It has been pointed out that Canadian manufacturing firms which are now on the English unit have an advantage over our competitors in those countries on the metric system. When we eventually convert to the metric system Canadian manufacturers will lose that advantage. That is another point we must consider.
Metric conversion is not a substitute for Canadian ownership which is necessary to export our manufactured goods. I know there is a lot to be said for an against conversion to the metric system, and I know we have to face up to this.
I understand the American Metric Association will be meeting at nine o'clock tomorrow in Washington to try to come to grips with this. The consumer goods industries in the United States will not move until there is legislation. We should be looking to the United States to see what legislation is put forward. There must be a benefit to the Canadian consumer, and this must be demonstrated in dollar terms.
I hope, as previous speakers have suggested, that the government will give consideration to introducing more than just a resolution. As was mentioned earlier, a bill on the metric system should be introduced so that this whole matter can be discussed both in committee and in the House. When this is done we can then move forward.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE PROGRAM OF GUIDELINE DATES FOR METRIC CONVERSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take this opportunity to criticize the government for proceeding on this matter by way of resolution. This has been done by at least the two previous speakers, including a former cabinet minister, the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray). It seems that whenever the government gets into a potentially difficult political situation, it tends to proceed by way of resolution to get out of its political problems.
We are supposed to be approving the activities of the Metric Commission which was approved by order-in-council. Except for some remarks that were made in 1970 when a white paper proposing something along this line was tabled, this House of Commons has not had anything to say about the establishment of that commission. I suggest that what has grown out of that bears no resemblance to what one could reasonably have expected to be the policy

of the government at that time. The order-in-council set up the Metric Commission to advise the government on how to proceed with the metrication of weights and measures in this country. I do not think that order-in-council would necessarily have led anyone to believe that legislation to protect the people of this country in the process of establishing metrication would never be produced.
We have before us a very brief resolution. It is to the effect that we approve the government's program of guideline dates for metric conversion. If this resolution is approved, and if the other place goes along with it, I can well imagine this government saying that this parliament generally approves of everything it has done and will do over the next four, five or six years in the implementation of metrication in this country, without any further reference to this House or the other place.
It seems this government is acting as the lackey of multinational corporations. I am surprised my friends to the left did not notice that fact because they generally go after the government whenever it does anything that might be favourable to the multinational corporations. We seem to be proceeding under assumption that what is good for General Motors is good for Canada. Those pushing hardest for this program are the members of the Canadian Manufacturers Association, which is bankrolled largely by General Motors and other manufacturing companies. I do not necessarily follow that philosophy. I generally agree with the policy of the Canadian Manufacturers Association, but not with regard to what they are proposing in the field of metrication.
We must remember that we are a part of a very large market, the North America continent. I believe it is of utmost importance to note what is happening in the United States. Attempts have been made in that country to pass legislation which would protect various elements of its economy. For one reason or another, they have not met with success. However, they are at least attempting to have legislation. Last year a bill which would have brought the process along faster was defeated in congress.
It is interesting to note that Mr. Gossage, the chairman of the Metric Commission, is not here today. It may be of interest to know where he is. I believe he is in Washington. I do not know whether he is getting orders or giving them. It appears that this government's action and proposals will be used as a lever to advance metrication in the United States because of our close ties, particularly in the automobile manufacturing industry.
I really do not feel amenable to being used as a tool to assist a process which is happening in the United States. In any event, even though that bill was defeated in the U.S. Congress, another effort is presently being made under the auspices of Senator Pell of Rhode Island. It does not seem to be making fast headway, but at least this legislation provides for reports to be made on the general progress which is going on in the area of conversion.
My hon. friend from Halton-Wentworth said the Commission has spent some $7 million. To be fair, I suppose it has not spent all that money yet, but it has probably spent in excess of $4 million. I should like to see some accounting of the manner in which these funds have been spent.

So far what we have seen looks like an ineffective promotion campaign. Canadians have certainly not been told what the effect of the program is going to be. The government is remiss in failing to ensure that the Commission should report to the House of Commons on its activities. It seems inconceivable that so large a sum could be spent when the only public result is the announcement that temperatures will be given in Celsius instead of fahrenheit in two weeks time. I have certainly heard no explanation as to the way in which the money has been spent.
Another feature of Senator Pell's bill is that provision is made for a regular report on the results and benefits of metrication. The government has left a gaping hole in this area. We have been given no estimate of what the cost of metrication will be to the country. Here we are, in a period of double digit inflation, and nobody appears to give a damn about what the cost will be. I would say this applies to practically everybody in the House of Commons because there seems to be no dedicated will to prevent the government from proceeding in this way. I hope there will be some opposition from this side.
The minister says he will be giving assistance to small businessmen who need it, though he did not spell out the details. I am sure that had we gone ahead with the government's original proposal no such consideration would have been shown. I should like to see more active opposition to this system of government by regulation. I think the opposition has been remiss in this respect. I hope it will change its view and seek to convince the government of the wisdom of trying to govern the country by means of laws, not regulations. It is true the minister has given us certain assurances, but his words are not worth a tinker's damn when it comes to protecting the people when the account is finally presented in respect to this process.
The United States bill also proposes that the commission envisaged in that country should have power to recommend additional legislation which may be required from time to time to solve the problems arising over the imposition of metrication. This is not a simple procedure, Madam Speaker. After all this deals with concepts. We all know that in a country such as ours, where there are two official languages, many difficulties arise because words which express a certain notion in one language do not, on translation, express the same notion in the other. When one is dealing in concepts it takes a special understanding if one is to get the idea across. When one is dealing in weights and measures, one is dealing in concepts. I have been listening to these Celsius temperatures on the radio for some months now-maybe I am a slow learner-I am learning French and possibly I am slow at that-but I am having the same difficulty in getting a true idea of what Celsius figures really mean.
Yesterday morning I looked at the temperature on the cablevision station to find out how cold it was. I saw the figures Ol but I did not notice the "c" for Celsius. I concluded it was going to be cool outside so I did not bother to put on my rubbers. On my way to church I met with a bunch of slush because it was above freezing point. This is the sort of thing that can happen.
In any event, there ought to have been an analysis of the economic impact of this proposal upon the country. Why give a blank cheque to the type of government we have
Metric Conversion
over there? We do not know what the cost will be. It has been estimated that the cost to the United States will be between $40 and $45 billion before the process is completed there. If the normal relationship applies, and our costs are 10 per cent of theirs, Canada will be faced with a bill of between $4 billion and $4.5 billion.
We heard a lot of talk about an Arctic pipeline to bring gas from the north. This is regarded as a tremendous undertaking. The Berger Commission will be sitting in Yellowknife for God knows how long, hearing representations of one kind or another. The National Energy Board or it agents, or those interested in the undertaking will spend millions of dollars before a decision is made about what will happen up there. That pipeline, I remind hon. members, is estimated to cost around $5 billion if the Maple Leaf route is followed. But a decision to proceed is subject to all sorts of complex procedures.
Here we are dealing with a proposal which could exert an untold economic impact on the country, and the minister comes along asking parliament in effect to give him a blank cheque. "Just approve what we are doing," he says. I cannot understand a government wishing to proceed in this way, and I cannot understand an opposition allowing a government to get off so easily.
As I said, there is a bill being presented in the U.S. Congress having to do with this subject. There is also supposed to be an administration bill presented by the government of the United States. So evidently the U.S. government feels it should proceed by way of legislation. Yet no such bill has been introduced in Canada. Why are we in such a rush to get ahead of the Americans in this regard if we are not acting as a tool for someone else to push the Americans along? Again, I would ask, what is Mr. Gossage doing in Washington tonight and tomorrow? I would also question what is being done with all the money that this commission has spent and is proposing to spend during the next year, totalling some $7 million, other than promoting the interests of large, multinational, manufacturing corporations.
The hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kem-pling) said that no minister of the Crown had said anything about this matter, but again I would have to correct him to some extent. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), who was here earlier this afternoon when the hon. member said that, did make a statement about metrication, and he said it was going to cost agriculture a lot of money. So there is evidence from that side. I wish the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) would pay a little more attention to the Minister of Agriculture when he makes representations about this matter, but apparently the Minister of Agriculture is being ignored by the rest of the cabinet.
The former minister, the hon. member for Windsor West, made reference to rip-offs and the fact that it would be easy for unscrupulous merchants to profiteer from metrication at the expense of the uninformed when the guidelines become effective. I think we must look at the experience of the United Kingdom in this regard, because in fact that is what happened there. Why is the government sponsoring a program that can make this possible,
28996 -6OV2
