and why has it made no effort at all to examine the experience of other countries and find out what happened there? We need some protection in this country against unscrupulous people who have shown the capacity to use metrication to bilk the public.
The government should bring in a bill, which would then make the subject of metrication a wide open debate in parliament. It would attract publicity and would focus the attention of the public on the issue. I admit that metrication has got to come; we cannot just remain an island by ourselves. I think it is a good thing, and all educators agree that it will be easier to learn mathematics and the sciences through the use of the decimal system. I am an exponent of the adoption of this system, but I am certainly not an exponent of having it adopted at any price; as I say, the people of this country deserve some protection in this regard.
What is required is proper debate of the question. I suppose the minister is surprised that we are still talking about this subject, that we have spent one whole day discussing a program that could cost $4.5 billion before it is completed. This seems to me to be a funny attitude to take. Even though the minister might feel that we are wasting time, I think he should take a proper approach and welcome a full debate of the issue in the House of Commons. This would serve as an educational tool, because there is going to be a great deal of resistance to metrication by people across the country.
I suppose I should not be advising the minister on how to look at this politically, but I can see not too far down the road another election in about 1978, which will be the crunch year for implementing the guidelines on metrication. It is then that people will observe that something is happening, and they are not going to like it. Naturally, no one likes change, that is human nature, so some time should be spent on education. This is one of my criticisms of this ineffective commission that was appointed two or three years ago-it has not done any sort of job of educating. It has conducted a glossy type of promotional campaign but very little real education has been involved. This is why I should have thought that the minister would welcome the opportunity for a wide ranging debate to educate the people of this country.
This brings to my mind another factor that is generally overlooked by the members sitting opposite. They seem to think that this country revolves absolutely around the cities of Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal, that there is nothing further east or further west of the golden triangle. To them, one day's debate in the House of Commons is a pretty big thing, and they have no conception of the fact that it takes time to get a message across to the people of Canada. I am just amazed that they adopt this attitude in regard to what essentially is a very fundamental and important matter to the economy of this country.
Secondly, a bill would provide the opportunity to examine the process of metric conversion in the House, and also perhaps in a committee of the other place. This would mean that witnesses could be questioned and might be able to offer something constructive to the process. Instead, we have appointed this very small commission which I guess has had a lot of volunteer help in its sector committees. Generally speaking it has not taken the

public into its confidence at all, but has just concentrated upon interested people in various trades and fields of manufacturing endeavour.
Thirdly, if instead of proceeding by resolution we took the legislative route to which we are accustomed here, it would provide a forum for interested parties with legitimate complaints, parties that I feel under our system should be given the opportunity to be heard.
Fourthly, as I have already said, this resolution does not bind the government in any way, shape or form. The minuscule assurances that the minister offered in his remarks this afternoon bind no one in the future. In addition, there is no way in which this resolution can be amended in any meaningful form. We are presented with a resolution which we can either vote for or vote against. I spent some time this afternoon discussing with others the possibility of framing an amendment that would attempt to focus on the need for legislation, but I found that there is practically no amendment that is in order that could be proposed. In other words, we are stuck with a proposal of the government, and with no room for amendment.
If the government had put a bill before the House there would be all sorts of opportunities to change and improve it. I have heard it said by many Liberals that this is one of the reasons why they are over there and we are where we are. They say we always take so much time examining the shortcomings of government legislation and proposing very constructive amendments to it that, by the time the legislation gets through, it is in such good shape that the Liberals get the credit for it, and so they stay where they are. They think we would be much better off if we did not criticize so much but took the legislation as initially offered. The fact is that for the proper orderliness of the House, and to get the best out of the House of Commons, proposals should be put before us which can be improved, and improvements can only be made by amendment. The silly resolution before us is just a blank cheque that is not subject to amendment.
As I said earlier, Madam Speaker, it is very important that we stay reasonably close to what is happening in the United States in regard to metrication. After all, almost 70 per cent of our trade is with the United States which, at least at the official level, is lagging behind this country in the introduction of metrication.
As far as the other 30 per cent of our exports are concerned, as said earlier by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie), only 8 per cent are subject to this business of metrication. So instead of making it easier for a large portion of our exports to enter into foreign markets what is going to happen is that we will wipe out this non-tariff barrier we now enjoy, and make it much easier for foreign countries which have had metrication for a long time and are advanced in that area to compete with our own industries.
This is why I believe General Motors and the large multi-national manufacturing companies want metrication imposed here as soon as possible, so they can then go abroad and obtain their components at much more competitive prices than they can here in Canada. All we would be doing by metrication without proper ground rules


would be subjecting our small manufacturers to much tougher competition from abroad. There should be legislation to protect our small business firms.
Foreign owned companies can increase their markets at the expense of Canadian owned small businesses through the metrication process. For example, Canada already imports more than half its machinery and equipment. We do not want metrication just to create a larger market for machinery imports from other parts of the world such as Sweden and the European Common Market. Conversion could increase the cost of production and supply in Canada, placing Canadian produced products at an even greater disadvantage on the Canadian market.
One objective of legislation would be to get Canadian owned small businesses through the metric process without financial hardship, so that Canadians will not only import less machinery and products but in fact will be increasingly world competitive and export oriented.
During the process of metrication there will be a period of overlap during which small manufacturing businesses will have to stock two inventories, one in metric measurement and one in the present measurement. That additional inventory will not be bringing in additional business. This will involve a non-productive expense, and bankers are not generally agreeable to lending money on things that are not turned over quickly. Whatever money is loaned will carry an interest rate that can only increase the cost of doing business.
It should be set out clearly what responsibility the government is willing to accept. The minister suggested that the Industrial Development Bank would help people get over this process. This again involves loans, and someone will have to bear the expense involved. There should be a system of grants to assist businesses in this conversion process.
There are innumerable other small headaches that will occur as a result of conversion. What will happen to existing equipment? How long are inventories for repairs going to be maintained, and who is going to pay the cost? Who is to guarantee that materials will even be available? Speaking as a lawyer who has been engaged in a fair amount of land conveyancing, it strikes me as being a big job to convert all our legal descriptions in the various land titles and registry offices into whatever acres are to become under metrication. It is probably fairly simple to convert a quarter section or a section of land, but what about the small parcels? I can think of untold things that will cause inconvenience and expense, and we do not know whether these things have been considered by the government.
I cannot state strongly enough that the government is proceeding in the wrong way with this conversion. This should not be done by resolution, which is just a blank cheque, but rather by legislation so we can see the actual results for the people we represent. I cannot support the government in its aim to have metrication take place by executive action without legislation. I would ask members of the House to slow the government down in its apparent haste to achieve its present objective.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE PROGRAM OF GUIDELINE DATES FOR METRIC CONVERSION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, a great deal of interesting and important information
Metric Conversion
has been placed before the House in the course of this debate. I do not propose that I am of a calibre to enlarge on the scientific era in which we exist, or the scientific evidence which has been placed before us, both for and against the metric system, by those who would discuss it. But there are a few things I do know about it, and I am acquainted with a few of its hardships.
There are three men I should like to see in this House at this moment as I think two of them would understand what I want to say, and the third might then understand better. They are the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald), who was a farmer, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who I think has very little knowledge or understanding of the hardships that uncontrolled metrication will bring about at the farming level.
There are certain areas where one can define with great accuracy the cost of conversion of a particular plant in order to make a new product in metric dimensions. That expense can be calculated. However, for the individual who uses a piece of machinery for decades-who has given that man consideration? There is a man who sits in this House who discussed with me the use of a tractor which is now some 30 years old. I would ask where that man is going to obtain parts for that tractor, made with English measurements some 30 years before metrication? What guarantee have we that these things will be available?
For years to come it will be absolutely essential that any farmer must have in his possession two sets of tools, and two sets of all the nuts and bolts he might ever require. He will have to carry them around in the field with him every day, because if he makes any effort to use metric tools on the nuts and bolts made by English measurement he will spoil both the nuts and bolts and the tools. There is too much play, and therefore they destroy one another.
Now if we go to the fishing industry, the lumber industry or the sawmill industry we find ourselves in virtually the same situation. It will mean that if they cannot get bolts for their equipment they will have to buy new equipment or take the old equipment to the machine shop and have it either filled in, bored out, or re-threaded to take the new bolts, or it may have to be drilled out in order that the bolts will fit. In machinery there is no tolerance for a misfit. There is no way one can say that a bolt can be within a millimetre of the required measurement because it will leave play in the machinery which will wear and destroy the whole structure of the machine.
The Prime Minister should remember that this is not simply a matter of changing the weigh structure of a scale. It is not simply a matter of changing die castings in a single factory. This can be done at a minimum of cost only if there is legislation to protect those against whom the long-range effects will cost hundreds of millions of dollars in this country. The amount has never yet been calculated by the three wise men from the east who act as the committee for the guidance of the metric system conversion under this government as it is being introduced in this country.
I plead wivh the government to have mercy on those who cannot convert today or tomorrow. I plead that there

Metric Conversion
be economic mercy in respect of these people because they need it. I plead that the fact be considered that it is not at all impossible in a seeding operation that there might be two machines in tandem, one made by the metric system and the other made by the English system, towed by a tractor made by the metric system. One definitely would need two sets of tools.
One farmer who is extremely well equipped with tools estimated that the minimum expense in his operation alone for the purchase of two sets of tools which he will need in the next five years will be not less than $1,500. There is a multitude of farmers in this country who will each spend $1,500 or more to re-equip their machine shops and tool cases. This expense has never been mentioned. There is a possibility of a reasonable evolution, but unless we co-ordinate this step by step, and move by move with the greatest trading partner we have, the United States, we will cost ourselves a great deal more money than has been mentioned by any speaker in this House today, or in any forecast by any government.
The cabinet and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) should not think just of shifting the beam of the scale. That is a small and final job. They should think of the guy who will live with change and inconvenience for decades. They should consider that he will have some equipment which is highly utilitarian around him which he cannot afford to replace for decades to come. I say: give us legislation and a plan; do not ask us to sign a blank cheque. I appeal to the government for once to please move on behalf of the little guy, not the big guy, the little guy in the woods and in the shop.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPROVE PROGRAM OF GUIDELINE DATES FOR METRIC CONVERSION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this evening we have heard a number of my colleagues discuss this proposal of the government. Not one objected to the metric system as such, or expressed doubt that we should have the metric system here in Canada. They have quarrelled, however, with the method by which we are going about this from the government's point of view. They do not criticize the work of the Metric Commission which is going on at the present time.
I must say I agree with my colleagues, the hon. member for Palliser (Mr. Schumacher), the hon. member for Carle-ton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) and the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), and many others who have spoken today, when they say that conversion to the metric system has such far-sweeping consequences that it must be done by legislation. There are many people who will have to be educated in respect of the practicality of the idea. Since man inherently hates change there will be resistance to change. We can imagine what will happen after April 1 when people will hear what the temperature is on their radios and TV sets only in metric or Celsius degrees.
Let me say in all fairness that there are ways of doing these things. I have just returned from Australia where they have chosen the castor oil method, as I would call it. There was a straight implementation; bang, there it was. They have had it for a little over a year. I did not hear one complaint about it. Instead of having a five furlong horse race they have a race of 12 metres. I am sure more people understand what 12 metres are than what five furlongs are, because outside of the racing fraternity you could ask
[Mr. McCain.)
anyone what a furlong is and he would ask, "What is that?" So, there we are. I do not think there will be any difficulty about this in due course.
However, in addition to what my colleagues have said about the necessity of legislation-and I will insist upon that and before I close my remarks 1 will introduce an amendment to that effect-we approve the guideline dates but subject to the introduction of legislation to govern the conversion to the metric system. There is no way in which we can rely upon statements of ministers in the House. Are decisions to be based upon some supplementary estimates somewhere? What integrity is there in that? Madam Speaker, if you want a reference to statements by ministers and the ability to rely upon them, I invite you to read the High Court of Justice decision in Ontario in the case of the Roman Corporation Limited and others versus Hudson-Bay Oil and Gas Company and others, including the Prime Minister and the then Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
The minister, or someone on his behalf, said that there would be some sort of small business assistance program with regard to metric conversion, and that there might be loans from IDB or some other body. That statement of the minister's is not worth a tinker's damn. I am not suggesting that that is not a bona fide statement, but there is nothing at all that commits the government to that statement, except perhaps for a political and moral commitment, but under the law it is just as if it were written in sand before a thunderstorm; it would disappear.
Certainly in the United States conversion is going forward, and I do not have quite the same fears as does my colleague, the hon. member for Palliser. I was in Washington a couple of months ago and I read in their papers that in certain schools they have already started to teach the metric system only in the pre-school grade and in the first year of school. In the other grades they teach both systems. They are phasing out the imperial unit system over a period of time. I have seen the metric system signs on their highways.
I invite government members who have not been in the House earlier this evening to read the speech of the former cabinet member, the hon. member for Windsor West, in Hansard in which he calls precisely for what we are calling, namely, legislation which will serve to assist small business concerns in making their conversion, either by loans or by grants, whatever it may be, and in defining certain guidelines of conduct. As the hon. member for Windsor West pointed out, the conversion from a quart to a litre, but at the same price, means an increase of 12 per cent to 14 per cent in actual profit.
There must be a wide ranging debate of the educational aspect, and agreement reached with the provinces with regard to the registration of land. At the moment-and I think the minister would quite candidly admit it-there is not one iota of agreement with any province with regard to land registry systems in any of the provinces and on the measurements whereby land shall be described legally.
How about that area in the west under the Torrens system, the compulsory land registration system based on the rectangular one mile by two miles, divided by road-

ways that are 66 feet apart? True enough, they happen to be 20 metres apart. Road allowances in western Canada fortunately will be 20 metres apart, but who will compel province A or B to convert to these guidelines within a timetable unless there is pre-arranged and pre-negotiated legislation? That is the point.
As a lawyer from western Canada I am appalled at the government going forward with this form of resolution and the House approving the guidelines without any legislation being put before us. How will the government bind, for instance, the government of the province of Alberta with regard to the conversion of the land registry system-by force of persuasion? Will it convert the province of Saskatchewan in the same way?
No one out there will oppose the idea of converting to the metric system. I know it is coming, and personally I welcome it. I think it is a much sounder system than the system under which we measure a length of cloth from the end of the hand of some long deceased monarch to the tip of his ear, or measure the height of a horse in hands, being the measure across a man's four knuckles. All of these things do not make sense. Of course it does not make sense to be out of step with the rest of the world. But the way the government is going about converting to the metric system could not be a more scatterbrained, ineffective or unlawful way of proceeding. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker):
That the motion be amended by adding thereto, next after the word "conversion", the following:
"but subject to legislative enactment of such a program by parliament".
I have copies of the amendment in both English and French.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-NIGER-ALLEGATION PEOPLE STARVING IN SPITE OF AVAILABILITY OF CANADIAN GRAIN-MEASURES TO CONTROL AID PROGRAM
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-NIGER-ALLEGATION PEOPLE STARVING IN SPITE OF AVAILABILITY OF CANADIAN GRAIN-MEASURES TO CONTROL AID PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on February 20 I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) if he had investigated a situation in the African country of Niger where bands of nomads are dying of starvation in a camp located ten feet away from the barbed wire compound containing a warehouse jammed with Canadian grain which is only available to local people with money to pay for it. The minister said that he had not conducted any such investigation but that he would look into this particular case and would be happy to follow it up.
I regret that it is now almost a month since the minister made that undertaking, but I will not use up seven valuable minutes raising hell over the fact that the question had not been given more prompt attention. Instead I will only indicate to you, Madam Speaker, my regret that this is but one illustration of the questions that arise concerning the entire CIDA program that need to be answered in order that the people of Canada can be reassured that their money is being well spent. I assure the minister that my information is very reliable concerning the particular incident that I cited. I would be pleased to discuss it with the minister privately if I could be of assistance, but he has not even asked.
I wish to return in a couple of moments to the question of bipartisan work in this chamber with respect to foreign aid and the development of Canada's international assistance program. The people of Canada today hear a good deal about food not getting through to the proper recipients in Bangladesh and certain African countries, and I think that we need to reassure them that proper steps are being taken to block off profiteering and black marketing which inevitably occur in recipient countries. Moreover, the Canadian people need to be reassured that food is not going to be used to prop up political regimes in recipient countries, and there have been instances where that has been the case.
That is really why the question I raised over this incident is an extremely important one. It is concerned not only with the distribution of Canada's food assistance abroad, important as that is, but it brings us to a consideration of all kinds of Canadian international assistance.
We have been hearing from the Secretary of State for External Affairs of the new phase Canada is going to enter with respect to its international assitance program. He brought in a report which he presented to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence last week in which he gave some detail about what I consider an important shift in policy by the Canadian government, in which the minister has indicated that he is moving the foreign policy of Canada into a new phase where, it is frankly stated, Canada must consider ways and means to expand our economic relations with the third world beyond aid. The new phrase we must put into the minds of the Canadian people for an understanding of this situation is "beyond aid".

Adjournment Debate
The interlocking set of global problems, the monetary instability, inflation, high food prices, and sharply increasing energy costs are at the root of the growing disparity between the majority of the world's people who are poor, and the minority who are rich.
Therefore the government has set up an interdepartmental committee headed by Mr. Robinson, who is the under Secretary of State for External Affairs, to bring together the various facets of Canada's international assistance program which include CIDA and food aid but which will go on to consider questions of trade and monetary reform as called for by the United Nations.
There will be the seventh special session of the U.N. General Assembly in September, at which I hope Canada will play a significant part. The very distinguished Canadian, Mr. Maurice Strong, who heads the United Nations environmental program, and who was a former head of CIDA, only yesterday came before the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence where he spoke movingly about his hopes for Canada's participation in the special session next September. He put in a nutshell the expectations and the goal which we as Canadians and, indeed, all the people of the developed countries should set as a minimum for the seventh special session. That goal is that there would be enough for every human being on earth in terms of food, shelter and clothing. That is a minimum need to protect human decency and dignity. With Mr. Strong, Madam Speaker, I say that anything less that that minimum goal is declaring bankruptcy in our civilization.
I have said that I believe this to be so important that we ought to go beyond politics in this House for a truly bipartisan effort to help Canada improve its over-all international development picture, which is why I have suggested that a subcommittee of the external affairs committee be set up to deal with a comprehensive policy for international development, and that perhaps it might work with the interdepartmental committee of officials who are working on this very matter. Indeed the Secretary of State for External Affairs said at the committee last week that he would not oppose the setting up of a subcommittee. When I raised a question in the House today, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that he sincerely welcomed any input by all members of this House into the improvement of the international development program of Canada.
I say to you, Madam Speaker, that we must be concerned about the sort of incident in Niger to which I alluded. We must reassure the Canadian people that these kinds of malpractices are being corrected, in order that the Canadian people will go on supporting CIDA, and its substantial budget for this year, and consider with open minds how we can enlarge our international development program. I say sincerely-and my remark is directed ultimately to the Prime Minister, and to the hon. member who will speak on behalf of the government-that we should work together on this program for the good of Canada and for the sake of human decency in the world.

speakeroldname: Mr. Herb Breau (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-NIGER-ALLEGATION PEOPLE STARVING IN SPITE OF AVAILABILITY OF CANADIAN GRAIN-MEASURES TO CONTROL AID PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I reassure the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) that I and other members on my side of the House

share his concern for developing countries of the third world. We think our efforts should include direct and multilateral aid, and that Canada has a part to play in making contributions to international and global organizations, and should, within those organizations, strive for a restructuring of trade, monetary aid, and other aspects of economics in order to provide a better break for the third world.
With respect to the question the hon. member raised tonight, I can assure him that, to the best of our knowledge, the nomads gathered in the refugee camps in Niger following the terrible drought in the past several years are not dying of hunger. They are, on the contrary, being taken care of by the Niger government, which is trying either to integrate them into a more sedentary way of life or, where possible, to enable them to resume their traditional way of life.
As for the second part of the hon. member's question, it is true that food depots are sometimes found close to certain refugee camps, for logistical reasons that are easy to understand.
Finally, the agreement between Canada and Niger is similar to bilateral agreements concerning food aid with other countries, in that the recipient country can either give or sell to local populations the products which we sent it. If the country decides to sell our food aid for reasons having to do with local market conditions or other considerations, it is authorized to do so on the condition that the revenues thus made be spent on development projects. Nothing leads us to believe that Niger is not respecting this agreement; the CIDA representative in Niamey reiterated the terms of this agreement last January to the Minister of External Affairs of Niger.

subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-BILINGUAL LABELLING-REQUEST FOR CONSULTATION WITH BUSINESSMEN-GOVERNMENT ACTION
CONSUMER AFFAIRS-BILINGUAL LABELLING-REQUEST FOR CONSULTATION WITH BUSINESSMEN-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when I first raised in this House a couple of weeks ago the question of Canada's new bilingual labelling laws, the minister said he would be making some changes. Although I, personally, did not receive notification of exactly what the minister was to do, I learned of his position from a newspaper report.
An article appearing in last Saturday's Winnipeg Tribune carries the headline, "Ouellet softens stand on new labelling laws." According to the article:
A new federal law regulating the labels on all merchandise sold in Canada, has been deemed too restrictive by Andre Ouellet, Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
Bill C-180, scheduled to become effective Sept. 1, 1975, requires that all products sold in Canada display the common name of the item in both English and French, and that any measurements be given in metric units.
After hearing complaints from small manufacturing firms and importers of goods made outside the country, Mr. Ouellet agreed that strict enforcement of the new law would create significant problems, resulting in undue hardship for some businesses.
I want to be on record as being concerned about this question. I hope the minister fully understands the many problems many small manufacturers across Canada will face if the program is implemented, and fully understands

just how inflationary the labelling laws will be if they are enforced.
The Winnipeg Chamber of Commerce presented a good case to the minister. The news report to which I just referred alludes to the brief presented by the Winnipeg Chamber of Commerce, of which the minister is aware. May I draw attention to an item which appears in that brief. The brief says in part:
As we understand it, it is possible that the Quebec Bill 22 may be tested before the courts and this whole subject resolved, but we are concerned that if in good faith our members design packaging to comply with the federal act and Bill 22 is upheld in the courts, particularly as it pertains to packaging legislation, we could be faced with another expensive redesign. In the circumstances, because of this uncertainty, we feel it would be prudent of the federal government to delay the implementation of Bill C-180 until this whole question of provincial rights in the area of consumer packaging has been clarified. We feel it is only fair that the federal government recognize that it would be impossible for our members to face the possibility of provincial legislation requiring different packaging requirements than does the federal act.
I now wish to quote from Canada's audio and home entertainment industry publication, "The Audio Retailer," as follows:
The application of Quebec's controversial new official language act could seriously affect the supply of audio goods in this province. Unless audio hardware is excluded from the provision of the act, most suppliers will withdraw from the Quebec market, according to a telephone survey of several Canadian distributors recently conducted by The Audio Retailer.
Products sold in Quebec "must be labelled in French, except within certain limits provided by regulation," states Section 34 of Bill 22. The audio industry must persuade the government to include hardware within these limits. Otherwise, in the opinion of Eric Blais, director of the Ministry of Education's French Language Office in Montreal, the act will be read to mean that front panels and control knobs, as well as warranties and instruction books, must be predominantly in French ...
"It's hard enough to get foreign manufacturers to meet CSA specifications, let alone make special panels," said Graham Bousfield of ReVox, and Hank Westerlaken of Panasonic guessed that the cost per unit of labelling a top-end line of receivers in French could be as high as $200.
Bill 22 is the most divisive piece of legislation that has ever appeared on a federal or provincial statute book. It makes a mockery of the Official Languages Act. It will seriously harm Quebec's economy with its ridiculous bilingual regulations, and make it most difficult for other countries and other parts of Canada to export merchandise to Quebec. The labelling and other aspects make it imperative that the federal government refer the matter to the Supreme Court of Canada to challenge its legality.
I have received many letters on this subject. I would like to point out how it is affecting small businesses in Canada. One of my constituents went to an embroidery shop to get some embroidery liquid. She wrote:
Adjournment Debate
-the shop told me it is no longer available because it is not worthwhile for the American producer to go into bilingual labels for his Canadian trade. The shopkeeper was so irate he took me on a tour of his shop pointing out all sorts of other items no longer available for the same reason.
I received a copy of a letter from a New York manufacturer to a Winnipeg importer. It states:
We would love to continue selling Canada, but there is no way possible that we could unless your government relaxes their regulations as our government has. We do comply with all government regulations in the United States. We therefore regret-

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-BILINGUAL LABELLING-REQUEST FOR CONSULTATION WITH BUSINESSMEN-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to remind the hon. member that the act passed by the Canadian government on packaging and labelling was first discussed in 1970. When it was passed by Parliament in 1971, it was supported by all parties in the House, including that of the hon. member. In other words, it was passed unanimously by the House of Commons.
To mix Bill 22 with that federal act is a great detour taken by the hon. member. I failed to see why the hon. member first wanted to protect the Quebec economy, finally I thought I saw in his remarks that he is against Bill 22. Let us not shuffle the cards: there is no connection between Bill 22 and that act which, in fact, gave ample notice to the parties concerned. The companies which produce goods other than food stuffs have had 18 months to take what steps are required to meet the requirements of the law. The food processing companies have until March 1976 to comply with the legislation, so they will have had a 24-month notice. I think that it is advisable to remind to the hon. member that the legislation will not apply in certain cases where a local manufacturer in a predominantly unilingual area makes a product exclusively used in that area.
I have recognized that some difficulties were encountered in the application of the legislation for imported products and I have explained at length in a press release issued on March 13 last-which can be appended to Hansard if hon. members want-the amendments which we are ready to introduce to facilitate the application of the legislation for some companies. More particularly, if the importers of those products are ready to relabel them according to the legislation before selling or despatching them to distributors or retailers, they would be allowed to do so when the products have reached Canada. It will thus be easier to comply with the requirements of the law. This is what I wanted to say, Madam Speaker. If I could obtain the unanimous consent of the House, those few paragraphs could be added to my statement.
